P2200.d: P2200 is the general electrical fault reported for the front NOx sensor on bank 1, the unit ahead of the SCR catalyst. Such sensors carry their own control unit, which checks the probe wiring and reports the result over CAN.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
No NOx value in live data from the upstream sensor
SCR or emissions warning, possibly followed by inducement countdown
c: Internal fault in the NOx probe or its attached control unit
Damaged cable between probe and sensor control unit (heat, chafing)
Moisture or corrosion in the sensor connector
Unstable supply or ground at the sensor control unit

P2201.d: Here the upstream NOx sensor on bank 1 is electrically intact, yet its reading is not believable. Manufacturers test this in different ways.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Often stored together with SCR efficiency codes such as P20EE
Increased AdBlue consumption or SCR warning
c: Aged or poisoned NOx sensing element with offset or slow response
Exhaust leak upstream of the sensor letting in outside air
Fault elsewhere (EGR, fuelling, DEF dosing) that shifts real NOx output

P2202.d: P2202 means the raw NOx value sent by the upstream sensor on bank 1 has dropped below the lowest figure a working sensor can report. Since the probe talks over CAN, the check concerns the transmitted value rather than a wire voltage.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Live data shows a negative NOx value upstream
SCR dosing may switch to a fallback strategy
c: NOx sensing element drifted low or internally faulty
Damaged probe lead or connector between element and sensor module

P2203.d: P2203 flags a raw NOx value from the upstream sensor on bank 1 that lies above anything the engine can actually emit. The limits differ: GM sets 1,500 or 2,500 ppm on the 6.6L Duramax (LML) and 2,500 ppm on the 3.0L LZ0 (Type B, two trips), VW 1,655 ppm on the 2014 Touareg TDI.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Implausibly high upstream NOx value in live data
Possible over-dosing of AdBlue or SCR efficiency codes
c: Upstream NOx sensor reading high due to internal failure
ECM software anomaly (GM 3.0L LZ0, bulletins 23-NA-193 and 24-NA-094)
Sensing element contaminated by oil ash or DEF deposits

P2204.d: P2204 describes an upstream NOx sensor on bank 1 whose signal path works most of the time but keeps dropping out. Smart NOx sensors report the state of their measuring circuit (open wire, short or no error) to the engine computer over CAN; when such fault messages come and go faster than a steady circuit fault would allow, this code fits.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on, sometimes going out again
NOx value in live data dropping out briefly
SCR warning that comes and goes
c: Loose or corroded terminals at the NOx sensor connector
Harness near the exhaust damaged by heat or vibration
Intermittent internal fault in the sensor module

P2205.d: The ceramic element of a NOx sensor only measures once its built-in heater has brought it to several hundred degrees. P2205 reports a break on the heater control side of the upstream sensor on bank 1.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after one trip
Upstream NOx sensor never becomes ready
SCR warning on the display
c: Heater element in the NOx probe burnt through
Broken conductor in the lead between probe and sensor module

P2206.d: A NOx sensor needs its ceramic element heated to several hundred degrees before it can measure. P2206 means the heater control circuit of the first (upstream) NOx sensor on bank 1 reads low, typically a short to ground or a driver output stuck low.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
SCR or emissions warning on the display
Usually no change in driveability
c: Internal heater or control-unit fault in the NOx sensor
Heater wiring chafed to ground near the exhaust
Moisture or corrosion in the sensor connector

P2207.d: P2207 is the high-side counterpart of P2206: the heater control circuit of the upstream NOx sensor on bank 1 shows a voltage that is too high for the commanded state, typically an open heater element or a short to supply voltage. CARB requires the diesel OBD system to flag such circuit faults that contradict the command.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
NOx readiness or SCR efficiency faults may follow
c: Heater element inside the NOx sensor burnt open
Open circuit or short to voltage in the heater wiring

P2208.d: Besides the control line, the NOx sensor heater has a sense or feedback path through which the controller checks how the heater actually responds (current, resistance or element temperature). P2208 marks a general fault in this sense circuit of the upstream sensor on bank 1.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
NOx sensor reports no valid value
c: Internal fault in the NOx sensor or its control unit
Damaged wiring between sensor element and sensor control unit

P2209.d: P2209 is the performance check of the NOx sensor heater: the feedback is electrically present but shows that the element does not reach or hold operating temperature as expected. VW's 2014 TDI specification books (Passat, Touareg) set it when NOx control has not become active more than 180 s after the dew point was passed.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
NOx sensor not ready for long periods after start
Possible follow-up SCR efficiency faults
c: Aged NOx sensor element that heats up too slowly
Low supply voltage or poor ground to the sensor
Prolonged cold or wet exhaust delaying dew-point release

P220A.d: A smart NOx sensor draws its own operating power, mostly for the probe heater. P220A means the supply reaching the upstream sensor on bank 1 is outside its window.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Upstream NOx sensor shows no value or no communication
Other NOx sensor codes stored at the same time
c: Blown fuse, faulty relay or poor ground in the sensor supply
Supply wire chafed, corroded or with high resistance
Supply booster in the glow plug control module (GM 6.6L LML)
Weak battery or charging-system voltage out of range

P220B.d: P220B concerns the second NOx sensor on bank 1, the one behind the SCR catalyst whose reading proves how well NOx is being converted. Its operating voltage is outside the allowed band.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Downstream NOx sensor shows no value
SCR efficiency monitor stays incomplete
c: Fuse, relay or ground fault in the downstream sensor supply
Supply wire to the rear sensor damaged under the vehicle

P220C.d: P220C is reserved for an engine with a separate exhaust path per cylinder bank, each with its own NOx sensors, and reports that the upstream sensor on bank 2 is not getting a proper supply voltage. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; the diesel pickups and trucks examined (Ford, GM, VW, Volvo/Mack) merge both banks into one SCR line and only use the bank 1 codes.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
No NOx value from the bank 2 upstream sensor
c: Fuse, relay or ground fault in the bank 2 sensor supply
Supply wiring to the bank 2 upstream sensor damaged
System voltage out of range (battery or alternator)

P220D.d: P220D covers the last position in this group: the downstream NOx sensor on bank 2, after that bank's own SCR catalyst, has a supply voltage outside its window. It only exists on engines whose two banks keep separate aftertreatment, which none of the publicly documented diesel applications do; no manufacturer lists the code with thresholds.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
SCR efficiency monitor for bank 2 not completed
c: Supply fuse, relay or ground fault for the bank 2 rear sensor
Corroded connector exposed to road spray behind the catalyst
Internal fault in the supply stage of the sensor module

P220E.d: P220E says the heater of the upstream NOx sensor on bank 1 is not behaving as commanded. Ford's 6.7L and 3.0L diesels bundle several checks under it: an open heater found by the sensor hardware, a short to positive (over 5 V on the heater), a short to ground (0 V), and a duty cycle that differs from the expected one by more than 20 percent.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Upstream NOx sensor slow to become ready after start
Often stored with P2201 or P2209
c: Aged heater element in the upstream NOx probe
Heater wiring or ground with high resistance or shorts

P220F.d: P220F is the heater check of the rear NOx sensor on bank 1, the one after the SCR catalyst. Ford's diesel summary (it titles the code as a heater sense circuit fault) flags a heater current under 0.4 A, a short to battery or to ground, or a heater duty cycle more than 20 percent away from the expected value.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
SCR efficiency monitor not completing
c: Heater of the downstream NOx probe weak or failed
Heater wiring of the rear sensor shorted or with high resistance
Water or salt in the rear sensor connector

P2210.d: P2210 means the heater feedback signal of the upstream NOx sensor on bank 1 sits below its permitted range. Typical electrical causes are a short to ground in the sense line or a failed measuring stage in the sensor electronics.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
No NOx reading in live data
c: Fault in the sensor element or its control unit

P2211.d: P2211 flags a heater feedback signal above its permitted range on the upstream NOx sensor of bank 1. An open sense line, a short to supply voltage or an interrupted heater element that the electronics reads as maximum resistance are the usual reasons.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
NOx sensor stays not ready
c: Interrupted heater element in the NOx sensor
Open sense line or short to voltage

P2212.d: Besides driving the heater, the upstream NOx sensor on bank 1 has a sense path that reports back how the heater actually responds; GM measures heater resistance on a separate HTemp pin. P2212 means this feedback keeps dropping out or jumping instead of failing for good.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on, possibly intermittent
Upstream NOx value briefly invalid
c: Loose or corroded contact in the NOx sensor connector
Cracked conductor in the probe lead that opens with heat or vibration
Intermittent fault in the sensor module's heater measurement

P2213.d: P2213 mirrors P2200 for the second cylinder bank: the NOx sensor serving bank 2 ahead of its SCR catalyst reports a general electrical fault. That presumes an engine whose banks feed separate aftertreatment lines.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
No NOx value from the bank 2 sensor in live data
SCR warning, possibly with an inducement countdown
c: Internal fault in the bank 2 NOx probe or its sensor control unit
Heat-damaged or chafed lead between probe and sensor control unit
Water or corrosion in the bank 2 sensor connector

P2214.d: Under J2012, P2214 is the plausibility fault of the bank 2 NOx sensor: wiring intact, reading not credible. No maker uses it that way in public documents.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Often stored with P2201 or SCR efficiency code P20EE
Higher DEF consumption or SCR warning
c: Aged or poisoned NOx element reading with offset or slow response
Sensor heater cracked by condensation (Hino 2015-2016, SB-15-038/SB-16-002)
Diluted DEF or faulty dosing injector distorting the NOx reading
Exhaust leak upstream of the sensor

P2215.d: P2215 says the NOx value transmitted for bank 2 falls below the smallest figure a healthy sensor can deliver. Because smart NOx sensors talk over CAN, the limit is a concentration in ppm, not a wire voltage.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Negative NOx value for bank 2 in live data
DEF dosing switches to a substitute strategy
c: NOx element of the bank 2 sensor drifted low
Fault in the measuring electronics of the sensor module
Damaged lead between probe and sensor module

P2216.d: P2216 is set when the NOx concentration reported for bank 2 exceeds anything the engine could plausibly emit. It belongs to engines with an SCR line per cylinder bank; none of the documented diesels is built that way, and no manufacturer lists P2216 publicly.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Implausibly high NOx value for bank 2 in live data
SCR efficiency codes may follow
c: Bank 2 NOx sensor reading too high due to internal failure
Sensing element fouled by oil ash or DEF crystals
Calibration error in the engine or dosing control software

P2217.d: P2217 describes a bank 2 NOx sensor whose measuring path fails only now and then: the reading drops out or the sensor briefly reports an electrical error, then recovers. A smart NOx sensor evaluates its own probe lines and sends status flags for open or shorted circuits alongside the value over CAN; flags that toggle point to this code rather than to the steady fault P2213.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp that comes and goes
Bank 2 NOx value briefly invalid in live data
c: Loose or corroded terminals at the bank 2 sensor connector
Lead near the exhaust cracked by heat or vibration
Sporadic fault in the sensor module electronics

P2218.d: A NOx sensor cannot measure until its built-in heater has taken the ceramic cell to several hundred degrees, and the sensor electronics switches that heater itself. P2218 reports a break in the heater control path of the bank 2 sensor, either inside the probe or in the lead to the sensor module.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after one trip
Bank 2 NOx sensor never reports ready
c: Heater element in the bank 2 NOx probe burnt through
Broken conductor between probe and sensor module
Pushed-back or corroded pin in the sensor connector

P2219.d: P2219 means the heater control line of the bank 2 NOx sensor is pulled toward ground when it should not be, typically a heater lead chafed against the exhaust or a shorted output stage in the sensor electronics. The control unit then switches the heater off to protect itself.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Bank 2 NOx sensor stays cold and delivers no value
c: Heater lead of the bank 2 sensor chafed through to ground
Shorted heater or output stage inside the sensor
Salt water bridging pins in the connector

P221A.d: P221A compares the two NOx sensors of bank 1, upstream and downstream of the SCR catalyst. When conditions should make both read alike, the gap between them is too large, so the system cannot tell which value to trust.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Often stored with P20EE or other SCR codes
Implausible NOx conversion values in live data
c: One of the two NOx sensors (often the outlet sensor) reading wrongly
Exhaust leak between the two sensors diluting the reading
Faulty DEF dosing distorting the comparison

P221B.d: P221B compares the NOx sensors before and after the SCR catalyst of bank 2. When operating conditions should make them agree, their readings differ by more than the calibration allows, and the controller cannot decide which value is wrong.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Often stored with SCR efficiency codes
Inlet and outlet NOx values for bank 2 disagree in live data
c: One of the two bank 2 NOx sensors reading wrongly
Exhaust leak between the two sensors
Dosing that does not stop or leaks, distorting the comparison

P221C.d: P221C reports that heater B of the DEF system draws too little current while switched on. GM and Ford both assign B to the heated pressure line that carries DEF to the dosing valve.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DEF line may freeze in winter, dosing starts late
DEF system warning, inducement possible if unresolved
c: Heating element in the DEF pressure line open or burnt
Corroded or loose connector at the heated line
Missing heater supply (fuse, relay or harness)

P221D.d: P221D is stored when heater B, the electrically heated DEF pressure line at GM and Ford, takes more current or power than its design permits. That usually means a partly shorted element or a lead touching ground, and the controller cuts the heater to save its driver.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after one trip (GM)
Line heater switched off, DEF may stay frozen in cold weather
c: Partly shorted heating element in the DEF pressure line
Water in the line heater connector

P221E.d: P221E says DEF heater C pulls too little current while commanded on. Which element is C depends on the system.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Slow DEF thawing in cold weather, dosing starts late
c: Heater C element open or burnt (tank or supply module, by system)
Corroded or wet connector at the tank or pump unit

P221F.d: P221F flags excessive current through DEF heater C, pointing to a partial short in the element or its lead. GM's 2025 Duramax tables, where heater 3 is the second tank heater, set the code above 15 A over 40 samples of 0.1 s whenever the vehicle is active, Type A with the MIL after one trip, and zero all heater PWM commands while any heater fault is present.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after one trip (GM)
DEF heating disabled, possible frozen-DEF warnings in winter
c: Heater lead chafed to ground at the tank or pump unit
Water or DEF crystals in the heater connector

P2220.d: P2220 is the high-side counterpart of P2219: on the bank 2 NOx sensor, the heater control line carries battery voltage when the heater should be off or regulated, so the element may overheat or the output stage cannot switch. A pinched lead touching a feed wire or a failed driver inside the sensor are the usual causes.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Bank 2 NOx reading missing or invalid
c: Heater control lead shorted to a supply wire
Failed heater driver inside the bank 2 sensor module

P2221.d: Alongside the heater drive, a NOx sensor has a sense path that tells the electronics how the heater is really behaving, usually by measuring its resistance, which tracks cell temperature. P2221 reports a general fault in that sense circuit on the bank 2 sensor.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Bank 2 NOx sensor not ready
c: Fault in the heater measurement of the bank 2 sensor
Open sense conductor between probe and sensor module

P2222.d: With P2222 the heater feedback of the bank 2 NOx sensor is electrically present, yet what it reports does not match the heating command: the cell warms too slowly or settles at the wrong resistance. No manufacturer documents this bank 2 code.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Bank 2 NOx sensor slow to become ready after a cold start
SCR monitor for bank 2 delayed
c: Aged heater in the bank 2 NOx probe with drifted resistance
Low supply voltage or poor ground at the sensor module

P2223.d: P2223 indicates that the heater sense line of the bank 2 NOx sensor sits at or near ground potential, so the electronics reads an impossibly low value for heater resistance. A sense conductor rubbed through to the exhaust bracket or a shorted measuring input inside the sensor module are the usual explanations.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
No valid NOx value from bank 2
c: Sense lead of the bank 2 sensor shorted to ground
Shorted measuring input in the sensor module

P2224.d: P2224 is logged when the heater sense signal of the bank 2 NOx sensor is too high, which the electronics sees as a short to supply voltage or as an interrupted heater reading near infinite resistance. The bank 2 code appears in no public manufacturer document.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Bank 2 NOx sensor stays unready
c: Heater element in the bank 2 probe open, read as maximum resistance
Sense lead shorted to a voltage source
Fault in the sensor module input stage

P2225.d: P2225 covers a heater sense circuit on the bank 2 NOx sensor that fails only for moments: the feedback drops out or jumps, then returns to normal, which a steady open or short code would not describe. No manufacturer documents thresholds for P2225 or for its bank 1 twin P2212.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp that comes and goes
Bank 2 NOx value briefly invalid
c: Loose or corroded contact in the bank 2 sensor connector
Cracked sense conductor that opens with heat or vibration
Sporadic fault in the heater measurement of the sensor module

P2226.d: P2226 is the general circuit code for barometric pressure sensor A, the sensor that tells the engine computer the outside air pressure for air-charge, fuel and boost calculations. Ford's OBD summary for 2024-2025 gasoline engines shows how the code appears in current software: every BARO fault is reported as P2226 plus a failure-type byte, -16 for a low voltage (formerly P2228), -17 for high (P2229), -92 for a plausi
s: Check engine light
Auto start-stop no longer works
Failure-type suffix (-16, -17, -92, -1F) shown with the code on newer scan tools
c: Fault of the barometric sensor built into the engine control module
Damaged wiring or loose connector on an external BARO sensor
5 V reference supply of the sensor pulled down by another faulty sensor

P2227.d: P2227 means the barometric reading is electrically fine but does not fit the other pressure signals. Ford's 2012 summary compares BARO, throttle inlet and manifold pressure after at least 10 s engine-off; the sensor that disagrees with the other two is blamed.
s: Check engine light
Reduced power or hesitation in very cold weather on turbo engines
P0299 or misfire codes stored alongside
c: Ice or sludge in the charge air cooler on turbo engines in severe cold (GM 22-NA-007, 23-NA-002)
BARO sensor reading with an offset or drift
Faulty boost or manifold pressure sensor that skews the comparison
Engine control software that needs an update

P2228.d: P2228 sets when the voltage from barometric pressure sensor A stays below the lowest value a real atmosphere could produce. Ford's gasoline summaries (2012 and 2020-2023) use under 2.0 V, which would mean an altitude above 15,000 ft, for 5 s; on these engines the sensor is mounted on the PCM circuit board.
s: Check engine light
Auto start-stop deactivated
Scan tool shows an implausibly low barometric pressure
c: Signal wire of an external BARO sensor shorted to ground or open
Defective sensor inside the PCM (Ford, Mazda and others), PCM replacement
Low or missing 5 V reference to the sensor

P2229.d: P2229 reports a barometric sensor A voltage above anything plausible for outside air. Ford's gasoline engines judge more than 4.4 V, an altitude below -1,000 ft, over 5 s; the 2023 diesels use 4.85 V (115 kPa) after 0.5 s.
s: Check engine light, often only after the engine bay has heated up
Auto start-stop deactivated
Scan tool shows barometric pressure far above the real value
c: Breather filter of a PCM-internal BARO sensor clogged (e.g. engine-bay wax, Mazda 01-008/20)
Signal wire of an external sensor shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
Internal fault of the sensor or the control module

P222A.d: P222A is the general circuit code for a second barometric pressure sensor, B. Only some engines carry one.
s: Check engine light
Usually no noticeable change in how the engine runs
c: Damaged wiring or corroded connector at sensor B
Fault in the shared 5 V sensor supply

P222B.d: P222B means sensor B delivers a clean signal whose value is wrong. GM documents two strategies.
s: Check engine light after two drives
Usually no driveability change
c: Sensor B reading with offset or stuck at one value
Leak or restriction in the intake path that distorts the comparison
Boost or manifold pressure sensor fault affecting the estimate

P222C.d: P222C flags a sensor B voltage that has dropped too low, as with a signal wire touching ground. GM's 2018 tables for the 3.0 L LGW set the code below 40 % of the 5 V range, equal to about 50.9 kPa, counted in 320 of 400 readings taken every 12.5 ms; it is a Type B fault with the MIL after two trips.
s: Check engine light
Scan tool shows a very low reading for the second barometric sensor
c: Signal wire of sensor B shorted to ground
5 V reference to sensor B open or shorted

P222D.d: P222D is stored when sensor B reports an excessive voltage. GM's 2018 tables for the 3.0 L LGW name contact with a supply voltage or a broken line: on that input a broken wire drives the signal up, not down.
s: Check engine light
Second barometric reading stuck near the top of its range
c: Connector of sensor B unplugged or signal wire broken
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage

P222E.d: P222E catches a sensor B signal that jitters. Outside air pressure changes slowly, so GM measures noise directly: every 12.5 ms the difference to the previous reading is taken, and the absolute differences over 80 consecutive readings are added up into a so-called string length.
s: Check engine light that may come and go
Second barometric value jumping on the scan tool
c: Loose or corroded terminal at sensor B or the ECM
Electrical interference, for example from a poorly grounded component nearby

P222F.d: P222F is meant for engines with two barometric sensors whose readings should agree but drift apart, without the software being able to say which of the two is wrong. No maker documents this code publicly.
s: Check engine light
The two barometric readings differ clearly on the scan tool
c: One of the two barometric sensors has drifted
Supply or ground offset shifting one sensor's signal
Blocked port or breather of one sensor

P2230.d: P2230 flags a barometric pressure (BARO) signal that is electrically present but jumps or drops out for short moments instead of sitting permanently low or high. The engine computer uses BARO for air-charge, fuelling and boost calculations.
s: Check engine light, often coming and going
Auto start-stop inactive
Other sensor codes stored at the same time if a shared harness is damaged
c: Engine harness chafed against an engine component (e.g. vacuum pump pulley, cam cover)
Loose or corroded pin at the BARO sensor or ECM connector
Barometric pressure sensor with an internal contact problem

P2231.d: P2231 means the engine computer sees the heater supply of the upstream oxygen sensor on bank 1 leaking into the sensor's signal path - typically an internal short in the sensor or two neighbouring wires touching in the harness. VW's 2014 specification books for the Passat and Tiguan set it when the front sensor signal changes by more than 190 microamps, i.e.
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption due to open-loop fuelling
Rough idle or hesitation in some cases
c: Internal short between heater and sensing element in the oxygen sensor
Heater and signal wires melted or chafed together (exhaust heat, routing)
Moisture or contamination bridging pins in the sensor connector

P2232.d: P2232 reports that the heater supply of the oxygen sensor behind the catalyst on bank 1 is bleeding into that sensor's signal line. A switching sensor only produces up to about 1 V, so the ECM watches its signal at the instant the heater is switched off.
s: Check engine light after two drives
Catalyst monitor not completed or catalyst code stored alongside
c: Internal leakage between heater and sensing element of the rear oxygen sensor
Signal and heater wires fused or chafed together near the exhaust
Water or corrosion bridging pins in the sensor connector

P2233.d: P2233 is the heater-to-signal short for sensor 3 on bank 1, a third oxygen sensor that some engines fit after a second catalyst or between two catalyst bricks. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Check engine light without noticeable driving change
Emissions inspection failed because of the stored code
c: Internal leakage between heater and sensing element of sensor 3
Sensor 3 wiring melted or chafed along the exhaust or underbody
Corroded underbody connector of the third sensor

P2234.d: P2234 means the heater of the front air-fuel sensor on bank 2 couples into its measuring circuit. On a wide-band sensor the disturbance is small, so the check is finer than on rear sensors.
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption when bank 2 runs without lambda control
Other bank 2 front-sensor codes stored at the same time
c: Front sensor element cracked by thermal shock (water on the hot sensor)
Heater and signal wires of the bank 2 sensor touching in the harness
Moisture in the sensor connector bridging heater and signal pins

P2235.d: P2235 concerns the post-catalyst oxygen sensor on bank 2, found on V engines with a catalyst per bank. The ECM sets it when switching off the heater makes the sensor voltage spike.
s: Check engine light after two drives
Bank 2 catalyst monitor not completed
c: Internal leakage between heater and sensing element of the bank 2 rear sensor
Sensor wires damaged by heat or chafing near the bank 2 catalyst
Water ingress in the rear sensor connector

P2236.d: P2236 would be set if the heater of the third oxygen sensor on bank 2 leaked into its signal wire. Such a sensor sits furthest downstream and exists only on engines with two catalyst stages per bank.
s: Check engine light with normal driving behaviour
Readiness for catalyst or oxygen sensor monitor not set
c: Internal leakage between heater and sensing element of sensor 3 on bank 2
Long underbody wiring to the rear sensor chafed or heat-damaged
Road salt corrosion in the sensor connector

P2237.d: P2237 points to an open pump-current line (IP or APE) on the front wide-band sensor of bank 1. With that wire broken the output freezes near its stoichiometric value of roughly 1.5 V and lambda stops moving.
s: Check engine light
Lambda reading stuck at 1.0 in live data
Higher fuel consumption in open-loop fuelling
c: Broken pump-current wire or pushed-back pin between sensor and ECM
Pump cell of the wide-band sensor damaged, for example by catalyst-heating strategy or thermal shock
Engine software that sets the code falsely (update available for some models)

P2238.d: P2238 is the low-side fault of the pump-current circuit of the front wide-band sensor on bank 1. Saab's 9-5 2.0 turbo (2010) shows a concrete test: on overrun with the injectors shut off, pure air should drive the signal well above its stoichiometric level, and if it stays below 1.7 V for 3 s the code sets as Type B.
s: Check engine light after two drives
Lambda value does not rise during coasting in live data
c: Pump-current wire chafed through to ground
Aged or contaminated sensor that no longer reads lean in fuel cut-off
Fault in the sensor interface of the ECM

P2239.d: P2239 is the high-side counterpart for the pump-current circuit of the bank 1 front wide-band sensor. On the Saab 9-5 2.0 turbo (2010) it sets when, in closed loop with the mixture deliberately enriched, the signal still sits at 1.48-1.51 V for 1 s, meaning the sensor ignores a change it should report; it is a Type B code.
s: Check engine light after two drives
Lambda reading frozen near 1.0 regardless of load
New sensor fails again quickly if the wiring short is not found
c: Pump-current wire shorted to heater supply or battery voltage
Wide-band sensor with internal short or stuck output
Damaged sensor interface in the ECM

P223A.d: P223A covers the control circuit of a fifth DEF heating element, heater E. Unlike heaters A to D, which each have four codes for open, performance, low and high, heater E gets only this one code, so any electrical fault of its driver or wiring ends up here.
s: Check engine light and SCR warning
DEF dosing delayed or blocked in freezing weather
c: Open or shorted wiring or connector of heater E
Heating element E burnt out or shorted
Faulty output stage in the controlling module

P223B.d: P223B reports a fault in the control circuit of heater F, the sixth heating element of an SCR system. Like its neighbour P223A for heater E, it is a single catch-all code covering open lines and shorts alike.
s: Check engine light and SCR warning
Reduced power warning after a cold-weather DEF fault
c: Damaged wiring or corroded connector of heater F
Heating element F open or shorted
Missing supply from the heater relay or fuse

P223C.d: P223C judges whether the pump current of the bank 1 wide-band sensor makes sense while the engine is coasting with fuel cut off. In that state the sensor sees almost pure air and, as Bosch's LSU 4.9 data show, must drive a clearly positive current.
s: Check engine light after two drives
Usually no noticeable change in driving behaviour
c: Aged or poisoned wide-band sensor with wrong pump current in air
Open pump-current, reference-cell or reference-ground wire
Exhaust leak or misfire that distorts the gas at the sensor

P223D.d: P223D applies the pump-current plausibility test to the front wide-band sensor of bank 2 on V engines. GM's 2016 and 2018 tables describe it for engines with a Continental interface chip: during a fuel cut-off window between 5 s and 12 s, a reading above 5.0 mA, within ±0.3 mA of zero, or below -0.10 mA is counted, and 40 hits in 160 samples in any window set the code as Type B.
s: Check engine light after two drives
Often no driveability complaint
c: Worn bank 2 wide-band sensor that no longer pumps correctly in air
Interrupted pump-current or reference circuit of the bank 2 sensor
Sensor heater too weak to keep the element at temperature

P223E.d: P223E checks the internal resistance of the reference (Nernst) cell in the bank 1 wide-band sensor. That resistance falls as the ceramic heats up, so the ECM uses it as a thermometer; Bosch specifies 300 ohms nominal for the LSU 4.9 at operating temperature.
s: Check engine light after two consecutive drives
Remote start refuses to start the engine (GM LTG models)
c: Aged sensor whose reference cell resistance has drifted
Heater not holding the element at temperature (heater, wiring or control)
ECM calibration fault on GM 2.0 turbo LTG (bulletin 16-NA-266)

P223F.d: P223F is the reference-cell resistance check for the front wide-band sensor of bank 2. GM's 2016 and 2018 tables translate the measured resistance into element temperature and count readings below 700 °C or above 1,000 °C; 64 of 80 samples (2018) or 128 of 160 (2016) at 25 ms set a Type B code.
s: Check engine light after two drives
Bank 2 lambda control slow to become active after a cold start
c: Bank 2 sensor ceramic aged and high-resistance
Weak heater supply or high resistance in the heater wiring
Sensor overheated by misfire or very high exhaust temperature

P2240.d: P2240 is the open pump-current circuit of the front wide-band sensor on bank 2, so it only exists on V engines and boxers. Ford's summaries (2012 and 2020-2023) introduced it to replace P0154; detection works as on bank 1, by lambda failing to react to reference-current pulses or by the NTK interface chip.
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 lambda value stuck at 1.0 in live data
Higher fuel consumption
c: Open pump-current wire or loose pin at the bank 2 sensor connector
Bank 2 front sensor damaged by water or thermal shock
PCM calibration that sets the code without a hardware fault (FCA 2025 Hurricane)

P2241.d: P2241 reports the pump-current circuit of the bank 2 front wide-band sensor at too low a level, typically a grounded wire or a sensor that cannot pump enough oxygen. No manufacturer publicly documents P2241 with thresholds.
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption from open-loop fuelling on bank 2
c: Bank 2 pump-current wire shorted to ground
Aged bank 2 front sensor with weak pump cell
Fault in the ECM sensor interface for bank 2

P2242.d: P2242 flags the pump-current circuit of the bank 2 front wide-band sensor as too high, usually a short to the heater feed or battery voltage, or a signal locked at its midpoint although the mixture is being changed. No manufacturer publicly documents P2242 with thresholds.
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 lambda value stuck near 1.0
Replacement sensor fails again if the short remains
c: Bank 2 pump-current wire shorted to heater supply or battery voltage
Internal short in the bank 2 wide-band sensor
Damaged sensor interface in the ECM

P2243.d: P2243 flags an open reference voltage line on the front wide-band sensor of bank 1, i.e. the Nernst-cell lead (RE/UN on Bosch sensors, VS on NTK).
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption from open-loop fuelling on bank 1
Catalyst efficiency code P0420 alongside it if a sensor fragment damaged the converter
c: Broken reference voltage (Nernst cell) wire or pushed-back pin between sensor and ECM
Sensing element cracked or tip broken off, for example by thermal shock
Engine software that sets the code falsely (update available for some models)

P2244.d: P2244 stands for a plausibility fault on the reference voltage side of the bank 1 upstream wide-band sensor: the Nernst-cell signal is electrically intact and within limits, but behaves in a way that does not fit the operating state, for instance offset or too slow. No manufacturer documents P2244 publicly.
s: Check engine light
Slightly higher fuel consumption
Possible failed emissions test
c: Aged or contaminated wide-band sensor (oil ash, silicone, coolant)
High resistance in the reference voltage wire or connector
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor distorting the reading

P2245.d: P2245 reports that the reference voltage side of the upstream air-fuel sensor on bank 1 reads too low, usually because the wire touches ground or the sensor has shorted internally. GM's tables for the Saturn Vue 3.5 V6 (L66, 2004-05) define it precisely: with the engine running for over 85 s, the heater active and the element signal between 3.2 and 4.6 V, a pump-cell circuit voltage below 1.5 V for 0.5 s stores the c
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption from open-loop fuelling on bank 1
Uneven idle or hesitation in some cases
c: Reference voltage wire shorted to ground (chafed against exhaust or body)
Sensor element damaged internally, for example by water hitting the hot ceramic
Fault in the sensor interface of the ECM

P2246.d: P2246 means the reference voltage line of the bank 1 front wide-band sensor reads too high, typically from a short to battery or heater voltage or a short inside the sensor. No manufacturer publishes a threshold for P2246.
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption
Repeat failure of a new sensor if the wiring short remains
c: Reference voltage wire shorted to heater supply or battery voltage
Internal short between heater and Nernst cell in the sensor
Fault in the sensor interface of the ECM

P2247.d: P2247 is the bank 2 version of P2243: the Nernst-cell reference line of the upstream wide-band sensor on the second cylinder bank is open. Ford's summaries trip it on Bosch sensors after 10 s outside 0.2-4.7 V and on NTK sensors via the interface chip, replacing the older P0150.
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption from open-loop fuelling on bank 2
Catalyst efficiency code P0430 if a sensor fragment damaged the converter
c: Broken reference voltage (Nernst cell) wire or loose pin on the bank 2 sensor
Cracked element or broken sensor tip after thermal shock
Engine software that sets the code falsely (update for some models)

P2248.d: P2248 is meant for a reference voltage signal on the bank 2 upstream wide-band sensor that is present but implausible, as opposed to an open or shorted line. No manufacturer documents P2248 publicly, and the published diagnostic tables of Ford, GM, Saab and VW cover the bank 2 Nernst-cell line only with the open-circuit code P2247, while Ford routes shorts to P0151/P0152.
s: Check engine light
Slightly higher fuel consumption
Possible failed emissions test
c: Aged or contaminated wide-band sensor on bank 2
High resistance in the reference voltage wire or connector
Exhaust leak ahead of the bank 2 sensor

P2249.d: P2249 indicates that the reference voltage circuit of the front air-fuel sensor on bank 2 is pulled too low, most often by a grounded wire in the harness or a fault inside the sensor. The only public manufacturer criteria come from GM's tables for the Saturn Vue 3.5 V6 (L66, 2004-05), a Honda-built engine: after more than 85 s of running with the sensor heater active and the element signal at 3.2-4.6 V, a pump-cell c
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption from open-loop fuelling on bank 2
Possible failed emissions test
c: Reference voltage wire shorted to ground on the bank 2 sensor harness
Internal short in the bank 2 air-fuel sensor
Fault in the sensor interface of the ECM

P224A.d: P224A concerns the heater of the upstream NOx sensor on bank 1, the one before the SCR catalyst. Its electrical resistance rises with temperature, so the sensor electronics use it to hold the ceramic element at working heat.
s: Check engine light
SCR efficiency or NOx plausibility codes may follow
c: Heating element of the NOx sensor aged or cracked
Corroded or loose contacts in the sensor connector
Unstable supply voltage to the sensor module

P224B.d: P224B is the heater resistance fault of the second NOx sensor on bank 1, mounted after the SCR catalyst. This sensor tells the control unit how much NOx is left after dosing, so its readings feed the catalyst efficiency monitor and the closed-loop dosing correction.
s: Check engine light
SCR efficiency monitor delayed or failing
c: Heating element of the downstream NOx sensor aged or damaged
Corrosion in the sensor connector exposed to road spray
Element cracked by water droplets hitting the hot sensor

P224C.d: P224C points to an open or otherwise faulty control circuit of shutoff valve A, the solenoid on a CNG or LPG tank that releases gas only when the engine runs on the alternative fuel. Such valves are normally closed.
s: Check engine light
Vehicle will not switch to gas operation or falls back to gasoline
c: Broken wire or unplugged connector at the tank valve
Solenoid coil of the valve open
Supply interrupted by relay or tripped inertia switch

P224D.d: P224D means tank shutoff valve A is electrically switched but the system behaves as if it stayed shut. Software can only infer that from a pressure response: once the valve is commanded open, line or rail pressure should climb toward the regulated value, which GM gives as 468-896 kPa for the bi-fuel Impala and Ford as about 724 kPa for its 2003 CNG trucks.
s: Check engine light
Engine switches back to gasoline or will not run on gas
Gas fuel gauge shows content although no gas is delivered
c: Manual tank valve closed or tank nearly empty
Valve plunger stuck closed, e.g. by contamination
Supply voltage too low to pull the solenoid open
Faulty gas pressure sensor misreporting the response

P224E.d: P224E sets when the control line of tank shutoff valve A reads too low. The DTC list of CNG upfitter TransEco Energy for its alternative fuel control module (AFCM v1.4) blames the line touching ground or being interrupted, turns on the MIL in both dedicated and bi-fuel setups and lets the system keep operating normally rather than forcing a fallback.
s: Check engine light
Gas operation unavailable or interrupted
c: Control wire of the tank valve chafed through to ground
Open circuit, which some modules report under this code
Shorted solenoid coil in the valve

P224F.d: P224F reports a control circuit of tank shutoff valve A that reads too high, typically a wire touching battery voltage. In TransEco Energy's AFCM fault list the cause is given as shorted to power, the MIL is lit and the gas system keeps working under the failure mode strategy.
s: Check engine light
Tank valve may stay open after switching off
c: Control wire of the tank valve shorted to battery voltage
Output stage in the alternative fuel control module stuck on
Wiring mistake after a conversion or repair

P2250.d: P2250 signals that the reference voltage line of the upstream wide-band sensor on bank 2 is too high, as happens with a short to the heater feed or battery voltage, or a breakdown inside the ceramic. No manufacturer documents P2250 publicly, and no bulletin in the NHTSA index names it.
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption
Repeat failure of a new sensor if the wiring short remains
c: Reference voltage wire of the bank 2 sensor shorted to heater supply or battery voltage
Internal short between heater and Nernst cell
Fault in the sensor interface of the ECM

P2251.d: P2251 points to an open negative current control line, i.e. the reference or virtual ground (VM on Bosch, COM on NTK) of the bank 1 upstream wide-band sensor.
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption from open-loop fuelling on bank 1
Possible rough running or failed emissions test
c: Broken reference ground wire or pushed-back pin between sensor and ECM
Internal open circuit in the wide-band sensor
Engine software that sets the code falsely (reprogramming for some models)

P2252.d: P2252 means the negative current control side of the bank 1 front air-fuel sensor reads too low, typically because that line or the sensor cell is shorted to ground. GM's tables for the Honda-built 3.5 V6 in the Saturn Vue (L66, 2004-05) describe it as a sensor-cell short: once the engine has run for 85 s with the heater working and the element signal between 3.2 and 4.6 V, a sensor-cell voltage under 0.3 V for 0.5 s
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption from open-loop fuelling on bank 1
Possible hesitation or uneven running
c: Reference ground or sensor-cell wire shorted to ground (chafed against exhaust or body)
Internal short in the air-fuel sensor
Fault in the sensor interface of the ECM

P2253.d: P2253 reports that the negative current control side of the bank 1 upstream air-fuel sensor reads too high. On the Honda-built 3.5 V6 of the 2004-05 Saturn Vue (L66), GM's tables treat it as an open sensor-cell circuit: with the heater operating and the element signal above 4.6 V, a sensor-cell voltage over 6.0 V for 5 s sets it, and P2256 does the same on bank 2.
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption from open-loop fuelling on bank 1
Repeat failure of a new sensor if a wiring short remains
c: Open sensor-cell wire or connector contact, letting the signal float high
Wire shorted to heater supply or battery voltage
Internal defect in the air-fuel sensor

P2254.d: P2254 concerns the negative current control line - also called reference ground, virtual ground or COM - of the wide-band air-fuel sensor ahead of the catalyst on bank 2. Ford's OBD summaries (2012 and 2020-2023) set it for an open line: with Bosch sensors the PCM briefly injects a reference current and flags the line if lambda barely moves, within about 10 s; with NTK sensors the interface chip reports the open line
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption from open-loop fuelling on bank 2
Possible rough running or failed emissions test
c: Broken reference ground wire or pushed-out pin between sensor and ECM
Internal open circuit in the wide-band sensor
Corroded sensor connector with high contact resistance

P2255.d: P2255 reports that the negative current control line (reference ground) of the bank 2 upstream wide-band sensor reads too low, typically a short to ground. No manufacturer publicly documents P2255 with thresholds.
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption
Possible hesitation or uneven running
c: Reference ground wire shorted to ground (chafed against exhaust or body)
Internal fault in the wide-band sensor
Fault in the sensor interface of the ECM

P2256.d: P2256 means the negative current control line (reference ground) of the bank 2 upstream wide-band sensor reads too high, typically a short to battery or heater voltage. No manufacturer publicly documents P2256 with thresholds.
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption
Repeat failure of a new sensor if the wiring short remains
c: Reference ground wire shorted to heater supply or battery voltage
Internal short in the wide-band sensor
Fault in the sensor interface of the ECM

P2257.d: P2257 concerns the control circuit of the secondary air (AIR) pump or its relay, which blows fresh air into the exhaust during cold starts so the catalyst lights off sooner. The code sets when that circuit reads low.
s: Check engine light
Secondary air pump silent during cold start
Secondary air flow codes such as P0411 may follow
c: Relay control wire shorted to ground
Secondary air relay with a shorted coil
Water ingress in the relay or pump connector

P2258.d: P2258 reports that the line controlling secondary air (AIR) pump A or its relay sits at too high a level, usually because it is shorted to battery voltage or the driver cannot pull it down. The pump only runs briefly after a cold start to heat the catalyst faster, so the fault mainly raises warm-up emissions.
s: MIL on, often without any noticeable change in driving
Secondary air pump silent after a cold start
Higher hydrocarbon emissions during warm-up, possibly a failed emissions test
c: Control wire of the AIR pump relay chafed through and touching a battery-voltage feed
Secondary air relay with shorted coil or welded contacts
Moisture or corrosion in the relay or pump connector bridging terminals
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P2259.d: P2259 is the low-level fault of the second secondary air control circuit, B. A second circuit exists where an engine uses two AIR pumps, two relays or a separately switched air valve; circuit A keeps its own codes P2257/P2258.
s: MIL on
Secondary air pump audible for longer than usual or while warm
Blown fuse of the secondary air pump after a long run
c: Control wire of circuit B chafed against the body or engine and shorted to ground
Relay or air valve B with a shorted winding
Corroded connector at relay B or the air valve

P225A.d: P225A concerns the front NOx sensor of bank 1, the one ahead of the SCR catalyst. Modern NOx probes come with their own control unit that holds a sensor-specific calibration and reports finished values over CAN; this code means the stored calibration data of that unit cannot be read or fails its check.
s: MIL on, usually without any change in how the engine runs
SCR dosing runs without valid feedback, so NOx emissions may rise
Follow-up NOx catalyst efficiency codes possible
c: Internal memory or checksum fault in the NOx sensor control unit
Replacement sensor with a part number or calibration that does not suit the vehicle
Supply voltage dropout or poor connector contact while the module was storing data
Engine or aftertreatment control unit software that misreads the sensor data

P225B.d: P225B is stored when the control unit of the downstream NOx sensor on bank 1 cannot provide valid calibration data from its memory. That sensor sits behind the SCR catalyst and is what the engine computer uses to judge how well urea dosing reduces NOx, so a sensor without trustworthy calibration leaves the catalyst monitor blind.
s: MIL on with no driveability complaint
SCR efficiency monitor does not complete or reports P20EE
Possible emissions test failure because readiness stays incomplete
c: Corrupted or unreadable calibration memory in the downstream NOx sensor module
Sensor installed with the wrong part number or an OEM calibration for another application
Moisture or corrosion at the sensor module connector disturbing its supply

P225C.d: P225C says the upstream NOx sensor of bank 1 reports more NOx than is plausible. Volvo describes its test on US17+OBD19 trucks: during engine motoring with zero fuel the engine makes no NOx, so the inlet sensor must fall below 50 ppm within about 10 s; each failure lights the MIL, which needs three clean drive cycles to go out.
s: MIL on, often without any noticeable driving fault
Code returns after the NOx sensor has been replaced
Higher DEF consumption or SCR efficiency codes in some cases
c: Engine or DEF control unit software that flags the sensor too eagerly
Leak in the charge air path or an EGR valve stuck partly open
Air mass or coolant temperature signal that skews the NOx model
Upstream NOx sensor with a genuine positive offset

P225D.d: P225D is the opposite case to P225C: the upstream NOx sensor of bank 1 reads too little NOx or refuses to rise when the engine should be producing it. Volvo and Mack list P225D among NOx codes where the sensor is very unlikely to be at fault, because the probe is simply measuring fresh air; their guide says not to replace it.
s: MIL on
Code persists after a new NOx sensor
Possible related intake, EGR or MAF codes
c: Charge air, intake or exhaust leak that lets the sensor see diluted gas
Sensor ports clogged with soot, for example after fuel contamination
Low-pressure EGR valve partly stuck open
Outdated engine control software that a published flash corrects

P225E.d: P225E points at the downstream NOx sensor of bank 1, behind the SCR catalyst, reading persistently high. Because that sensor sees what is left after urea dosing, a high value can be a sensor offset or genuine NOx slipping through a weak catalyst, poor DEF or a faulty dosing valve.
s: MIL on, often together with P20EE
Increased DEF consumption or DEF quality warnings
Power reduction possible if SCR efficiency codes follow
c: Real NOx slip from a weak SCR catalyst, poor DEF quality or a faulty dosing valve
Downstream NOx sensor with a positive offset
Control software that evaluates the sensor incorrectly

P225F.d: P225F is set when the downstream NOx sensor of bank 1 reports less NOx than expected or does not move away from a low value. A sensor behind the SCR catalyst that reads too low makes the catalyst look better than it is, so the efficiency monitor can no longer be trusted.
s: MIL on
SCR efficiency cannot be confirmed, readiness may stay open
c: Exhaust leak upstream of the downstream sensor drawing in outside air
Chafed or corroded wiring between sensor module and probe
Downstream NOx sensor with reduced sensitivity

P2260.d: P2260 flags secondary air control circuit B sitting at too high a level, as with a short to the supply or a driver output that cannot switch. Circuit B drives the second pump, second relay or a separate air valve, depending on the engine.
s: MIL on
Second secondary air pump or valve does not operate after a cold start
Increased cold-start emissions, possibly with a secondary air flow code on one bank
c: Control wire of circuit B shorted to a battery-voltage feed
Relay or air valve B with an open coil, depending on how the driver is diagnosed
Output stage for circuit B in the engine control module defective

P2261.d: P2261 means bypass valve A of the turbocharger or supercharger, also called the recirculation valve, does not work mechanically. When the throttle snaps shut it should let charge air flow back to the compressor inlet so the compressor does not surge.
s: Fluttering, chuffing or rattling noise from the turbo when lifting off the throttle
MIL on
Slightly delayed boost after gear changes
c: Bypass/recirculation valve sticking closed or with a torn diaphragm
Kinked, collapsed or wrongly routed recirculation or control hose
Electrical fault at the valve solenoid or its connector that prevents opening
Engine control module output reacting wrongly (software or hardware)

P2262.d: P2262 says boost pressure A does not appear at all although the charging system should be producing it, and the cause appears to be mechanical rather than a sensor fault. The control unit sees the pressure after the compressor stay near ambient or close to manifold pressure.
s: Clear loss of power, no turbo or supercharger pull
MIL on, often with a reduced-power mode
Hissing or whistling from the intake if a hose has come off
c: Intake or charge-air hose disconnected or split, so the compressor cannot build pressure
Wastegate or bypass stuck open, corroded or with a broken linkage
Damaged turbocharger or supercharger (bearing wear, broken drive, wheel damage)
Boost pressure sensor or its hose blocked or detached

P2263.d: P2263 means boost pressure measured in the intake manifold stays too far from the target set by the closed-loop boost control. CARB requires diesel OBD to detect underboost, overboost and slow response of the boost control.
s: Power loss or limp mode
Hissing or whistling from the charge-air system
Black smoke under load
c: Charge-air hose or cooler duct leaking or pulled off
Restricted exhaust, for example a heavily loaded particulate filter

P2264.d: P2264 is the general circuit code for water-in-fuel sensor A, the probe in the diesel filter or separator that detects water by its conductivity. GM's 2018 diesel tables explain a neat self-test: after the ignition has been off for more than about 8 h, a healthy sensor briefly signals water during the first 0.3 to 1.8 s after power-up.
s: Service lamp or message on, engine runs normally
No warning if water actually collects in the separator
c: Water-in-fuel sensor that no longer performs its power-up self-test
Corroded or loose connector at the filter housing, exposed to road spray
Open or damaged wire between sensor and ECM or tank zone module
Incompatible sensor fitted during a filter change

P2265.d: P2265 means the signal from water-in-fuel sensor A is electrically present but does not behave plausibly, for example a self-test response that comes at the wrong time or a value that sits between the expected dry and wet states. No manufacturer documents P2265 publicly.
s: Water warning or service lamp that comes and goes
Water warning stays on even after the filter has been drained
c: Sludge, emulsion or deposits coating the sensor electrodes
Sensor electronics drifting so the output lies between dry and wet
Corroded terminals adding resistance to the signal circuit

P2266.d: P2266 is set when the signal line of water-in-fuel sensor A stays below its valid range, typical of a grounded signal wire or of a conductive path that should not be there. Ford documents the code on 2017 and 2018 Super Duty trucks with the 6.7L diesel built up to 15 March 2018: bulletin 18-2133 links P2266, P2269 and P1140 with a lit water-in-fuel lamp to water entering connector C3080 at the sensor, which sits betw
s: Water-in-fuel lamp on although no water is in the separator
Often stored together with P2269
c: Water intrusion into the sensor connector bridging signal and ground
Sensor with internal resistance outside specification
Signal wire chafed against the frame and shorted to ground

P2267.d: P2267 reports that the signal of water-in-fuel sensor A sits above its valid range, which usually indicates an open signal or ground path, a disconnected sensor or a short to a voltage source. Stellantis has a case file for 2025 and 2026 Ram 2500 to 5500 trucks with the Cummins 6.7L: after the fuel filter module has been drained, the warning lamp may stay on with P2267 and P2269.
s: Water-in-fuel lamp stays on after draining
Often appears together with P2269
c: Residual contamination on the probes after draining the filter
Unplugged sensor or open signal or ground wire
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage

P2268.d: P2268 is reserved for a water-in-fuel sensor A circuit whose signal drops out or jumps for short moments instead of staying at a fault level. No manufacturer documents P2268 publicly.
s: Water warning flickers or appears briefly while driving
Code stored as history with no fault present at the workshop
c: Loose or corroded connector at the filter housing losing contact under vibration
Wire chafing intermittently near the frame or filter bracket
Moisture in the plug that changes with temperature and spray

P2269.d: P2269 is not a wiring fault but a statement about the fuel: sensor A has detected water. On diesels it means the separator is full; Ram's 2025-26 Cummins 6.7L trucks set it with the MIL, and Stellantis traced a persistent case to incomplete draining, fixed by draining and swapping the sensor's signal and ground pins (TSB 14-004-26).
s: Water-in-fuel lamp or message, on some vehicles also the MIL
Rough running, power loss or hard starting if water reaches the injection system
Reduced power on some engines to protect the injection system
c: Water separator full and not drained at the service interval
Fuel from the tank or filling station containing water
Residual water after draining or a wet sensor connector faking the alarm
Engine control software needing an update

P226A.d: P226A concerns the output that switches the water-in-fuel warning lamp, not the sensor. The control unit drives the lamp circuit and checks it electrically; an open lamp, a broken wire or a shorted driver lets it set this code.
s: Water-in-fuel lamp does not light during the bulb check at ignition on
Lamp stays on permanently regardless of the filter state
c: Burnt-out warning lamp or corroded lamp socket
Open or shorted wire between control unit and lamp
Faulty lamp driver in the control unit

P226B.d: P226B reports boost from turbocharger or supercharger A rising too high for a mechanical reason, for instance a wastegate or bypass that will not open or a seized actuator linkage, rather than a sensor or wiring fault. VW's 2014 book for the supercharged Touareg 3.0 TSI sets it when boost passes 250 kPa.
s: Sudden power cut or reduced-power mode under load
MIL on
Unusually strong surge of power just before the cut
c: Wastegate flap seized closed by corrosion or carbon
Seized or misadjusted wastegate or VGT actuator linkage
Vacuum or pressure line to a pneumatic actuator leaking or blocked

P226C.d: P226C means the boost control actuator of turbocharger A does move, but too slowly, so boost lags behind changes in demand. Ford's 2023 diesel summary runs an intrusive check on the 3.0 L and 1.5 L at idle, once in each drive cycle: the variable vanes travel from closed to open, and within 7 s manifold pressure must change by at least 6.5 kPa at sea level (3.5 kPa at 8,000 ft).
s: Hesitant pull from low engine speed, turbo lag
MIL on, sometimes with a torque limit
More smoke on acceleration with diesel engines
c: Variable vanes or turbine control valve sluggish from soot, varnish or corrosion
Worn electric or pneumatic boost actuator, or a weak control solenoid
Damaged wiring or connector between actuator and control module
Control module software that needs an update (cold-weather false sets)

P226D.d: P226D means the bank 1 particulate filter offers so little flow resistance that its core is likely broken, burnt out or removed. CARB requires detection of a destroyed or missing substrate, or a filter replaced by a pipe.
s: MIL on
Visible soot at the tailpipe if the filter core is damaged
Often no driveability change; regeneration behaviour may be affected
c: Filter core cracked, melted after an overheated regeneration, or removed
Differential pressure line disconnected, cracked, blocked or routed wrongly
Control software that sets the code without a hardware fault
Incorrect or faulty differential pressure sensor assembly

P226E.d: P226E reports a damaged or missing particulate filter core on bank 2, which only exists where each cylinder bank has its own filter. Ford documents it in its 2024-2025 OBD summary for petrol engines: the gasoline particulate filter check runs once the filter has been above 250 °C for 30 s and exhaust flow lies between 300 and 850 m³/h; if the lowest measured back pressure stays below the missing-brick threshold, a ra
s: MIL on
Usually no noticeable change in driving behaviour
c: Bank 2 filter core cracked, melted or removed
Pressure sensing line of bank 2 loose, cracked or blocked
Back pressure sensor reading too low

P226F.d: P226F is the slow-response fault of boost control B, meaning the actuator of a second turbocharger or of the second stage on twin-turbo, bi-turbo or sequential layouts. Which unit the letter B denotes is up to the manufacturer.
s: Delayed boost in the speed range where the second charger takes over
MIL on, possibly with reduced power
c: Boost actuator of turbocharger B sluggish or worn
Carbon or varnish restricting vanes or flap on turbocharger B
Leaking vacuum line or damaged wiring to actuator B

P2270.d: P2270 concerns the oxygen sensor behind the catalyst on bank 1. When the mixture turns rich, this sensor should rise to a high voltage; if it stays low, the ECM treats it as biased or stuck lean and can no longer rely on it for catalyst monitoring or the post-catalyst trim.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Catalyst and oxygen sensor readiness not completing
Usually no noticeable change in driveability
c: Rear oxygen sensor aged, contaminated or slow to reach rich voltage
Exhaust leak ahead of the rear sensor diluting the gas with air
Oil in the sensor connector or a bent terminal
Calibration issue fixed by an ECM update

P2271.d: P2271 is the opposite fault of the same bank 1 rear sensor: its voltage refuses to fall when the exhaust should be lean. It is usually checked during a deceleration fuel cut, when almost pure air passes the sensor.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Catalyst monitor not completing
c: Rear oxygen sensor contaminated by coolant, oil or silicone
Faulty front A/F sensor making the rear sensor look stuck rich
Signal wire chafed against a voltage source

P2272.d: P2272 applies to V and flat engines with a separate catalyst and rear oxygen sensor on bank 2; that sensor fails to reach a rich reading when the ECM enriches bank 2. GM's 2016 tables (16OBDG05) set it if the voltage is still under 800 mV after 68 g of air during forced enrichment (Type B).
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Catalyst monitor for bank 2 not completing
c: Bank 2 rear oxygen sensor aged or contaminated
Engine oil in the sensor connector, for example from a leaking oil pressure switch
Exhaust leak on bank 2 ahead of the rear sensor

P2273.d: P2273 means the rear oxygen sensor of bank 2 keeps a high voltage when the exhaust of that bank should be lean. GM's 2016 tables (16OBDG05) check this in fuel cut-off and set the code if the signal is above 100 mV after 9 g of air (Type B); GM's 2024 tables (24OBDG07) compare the lowest voltage during a commanded lean phase with 0.20 V over two trips.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Catalyst monitor for bank 2 not completing
c: Bank 2 rear oxygen sensor fouled by oil or coolant
Signal wire touching a supply or heater line
Bank 2 front sensor misreading so that the bank actually runs rich

P2274.d: Sensor 3 exists only where a bank has a third oxygen sensor, usually behind a second catalyst, so that sensor 2 sits between two bricks. P2274 says this last sensor on bank 1 stays lean when it should swing rich.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
No noticeable change in driveability
c: Third oxygen sensor aged or cracked by thermal shock from water
Exhaust leak ahead of sensor 3 drawing in air
Damaged wiring or connector of sensor 3

P2275.d: P2275 is the rich-side fault of the third oxygen sensor on bank 1, the last one on systems with two catalysts in series: it keeps a high voltage while the exhaust should be lean. VW's 2014 data books for the CC, Passat and Tiguan check it in fuel cut-off, comparing the voltage with 0.15 V once 4500 mg of oxygen have passed, more than the 3000 mg used for sensor 2 because the extra catalyst stores oxygen first.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
No noticeable change in driveability
c: Third oxygen sensor contaminated or damaged by water
Signal wire of sensor 3 touching a voltage source

P2276.d: P2276 needs three oxygen sensors on bank 2, so it only occurs on V or flat engines whose second bank carries a front, a mid-catalyst and a post-catalyst sensor. It reports that the post-catalyst sensor of bank 2 does not reach a rich reading.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
No noticeable change in driveability
c: Bank 2 third oxygen sensor aged or cracked by water
Exhaust leak on bank 2 ahead of sensor 3
Damaged wiring or connector of sensor 3

P2277.d: P2277 is the rich-side counterpart of P2276: the third, post-catalyst sensor on bank 2 does not drop to a lean reading. On such layouts the check normally runs during a fuel cut, when the second catalyst must fill with oxygen before the sensor can respond, so a slow or fouled element shows up here.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
No noticeable change in driveability
c: Bank 2 third oxygen sensor contaminated or water-damaged
Signal wire of sensor 3 touching a voltage source

P2278.d: P2278 reports that the third oxygen sensors of the two banks are connected the wrong way round, so the ECM reads the bank 1 sensor as if it sat on bank 2 and vice versa. The check changes the exhaust of one bank only, for example by cutting its injectors or feeding air into one exhaust line, and watches which sensor answers.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Catalyst or sensor codes reported for the wrong bank
c: Sensor 3 connectors of both banks plugged in crosswise after a repair
Harness routed to the wrong side or pins swapped in a connector
Wrong harness, ECM or calibration after a replacement

P2279.d: P2279 means the ECM has concluded that air enters the engine without being measured or expected, for example because the air mass sensor, manifold pressure and throttle position no longer agree with its air model. Volkswagen and Audi use it widely.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Whistling at idle, unstable or high idle speed
Limp mode on some engines
c: Leaking crankcase breather or PCV pressure-regulating valve
Leak at intake manifold, hoses or seals after the air mass sensor

P227A.d: P227A is the general circuit fault of barometric pressure sensor C, used when the control unit finds the signal missing or unusable without classifying it as too low or too high. Sensor C is not necessarily a separate ambient sensor: in GM's 2018 diesel tables the BARO C channel belongs to the turbocharger inlet pressure sensor, GM also uses it on the supercharged 6.2 L LT4, and on its 2023-2024 twin-throttle engine
s: MIL on
Usually no noticeable change in driving; slight power loss at altitude possible
c: Loose connector, corroded pins or damaged wiring at sensor C
5 V reference or sensor ground shared with other sensors disturbed

P227B.d: P227B means sensor C supplies an electrically sound signal that does not agree with the other pressure readings. In GM's 2018 diesel tables sensor C is the turbocharger inlet pressure sensor: the ECM compares it with BARO and MAP at idle and in the window between key-off and the next start, and if only sensor C is out of line it gets the blame, as a Type B fault after 320 failures in 400 samples.
s: MIL on
Mostly no driveability change; occasionally reduced boost
c: Sensor C drifting or with an offset
Sensor port blocked by dirt, oil or ice, or sensor not seated in its bore
Heavily clogged air filter shifting the pressure ahead of the compressor or throttle

P227C.d: P227C flags a voltage from pressure sensor C that is too low. GM's 2018 tables show two variants.
s: MIL on, on some engines immediately
Engine runs on a substitute value, at most slightly less power
c: Signal wire of sensor C shorted to ground
Open signal or 5 V supply line on inputs that read an open circuit as low
Replacement control module without the calibration that matches the fitted sensor

P227D.d: P227D is the high-voltage counterpart of P227C. On GM's 2018 diesel the sensor C input has a pull-up, so both a short to the supply and a broken signal wire push it above 90.2 % of 5 V (about 115.4 kPa); after 320 failures in 400 samples it is a Type B fault.
s: MIL on
Little change in driving; possibly reduced boost or poorer altitude compensation
c: Signal wire of sensor C shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
Broken signal wire or sensor ground on inputs with pull-up

P227E.d: P227E covers a sensor C signal that jumps although every single value is in range. GM measures this as a string length: the absolute difference between each reading and the one taken 12.5 ms earlier is summed over 80 consecutive readings, and a sum above 152 kPa (2018 diesel) or 150 kPa (supercharged LT4) counts as a failure.
s: MIL on, possibly coming and going
Occasional brief hesitation or uneven boost
c: Loose or corroded terminals in the sensor C connector
Interference from ignition or actuator wiring routed nearby
Sensor C with an unstable internal element

P227F.d: P227F means the passage between the air filter and the mass air flow sensor of bank 2 is restricted or lets air in that has bypassed the filter. By today's wording the code belongs to engines with a separate air path and MAF per bank; P2280 is the bank 1 version.
s: MIL on, on some trucks with an air filter service message
Reduced power and boost under load
More black smoke on diesel engines
c: Air filter clogged with dust or soaked with too much oil
Intake opening blocked by snow, leaves or a collapsed duct
Loose clamp or cracked duct between filter box and MAF on bank 2
Faulty filter restriction or inlet pressure sensor

P2280.d: P2280 is the bank 1 code for restricted airflow or an air leak between the air filter and the MAF sensor. A blocked filter lowers the pressure ahead of the sensor and limits the air the engine can take in.
s: MIL on
Less power and slower boost build-up under load
More smoke from diesel engines when accelerating
c: Air filter clogged or soaked with oil
Snow, ice or debris in the air inlet, or a collapsed intake duct
Cracked duct or loose clamp between filter box and MAF
Early software that flags the condition too readily

P2281.d: P2281 points to air that escapes or enters between the MAF sensor and the throttle body, so the airflow the sensor reports no longer matches what reaches the cylinders. On turbocharged engines this section includes the compressor, the charge air cooler and their hoses: a loose clamp or split boot can blow off charge air under boost or draw in unmeasured air at idle.
s: MIL on
Hissing under boost and less power
Black smoke on diesels or rough idle on petrol engines
c: Loose clamp, split hose or leaking charge air cooler between MAF and throttle
Contaminated or drifting MAF sensor that misreports airflow
Engine software that sets the code without a real leak (update available)
Disconnected crankcase vent or other hose joined to this section

P2282.d: P2282 means air enters the intake behind the throttle, so it reaches the cylinders without passing the throttle. Ford uses it as its PCV monitor on turbo engines with speed density: airflow worked out from manifold pressure is compared with airflow through the throttle, and a calculated leak of 1 lb/min or more for at least 5 s, with the throttle at 4 degrees or less, sets the code (2012, 2020-2023 and 2024 summaries
s: High or unstable idle speed
MIL on, sometimes with a hissing noise from the engine bay
Harder brake pedal if the brake vacuum line is affected
c: Brake booster vacuum pipe detached or its check valve stuck open
Crankcase ventilation hose disconnected or cracked
Leaking intake manifold gasket, throttle body seal or vacuum hose
Iced manifold pressure sensor or software miscalculating the leak

P2283.d: P2283 is the general circuit code for the injector control pressure (ICP) sensor. ICP describes the high-pressure engine oil that hydraulically actuated unit injectors (HEUI) use to pressurise fuel, as on Navistar-built Ford Power Stroke diesels; the sensor reports rail pressure so the injection pressure regulator can be closed-loop controlled.
s: Low power and hesitation
Hard or long cranking, especially when hot
MIL on
c: Failed ICP sensor, often with oil inside the connector
Damaged signal, reference or ground wire of the sensor
5-volt reference circuit pulled down by another sensor

P2284.d: P2284 means the measured injector control pressure does not follow what the PCM commands. Ford's 6.0L Power Stroke summaries (2003 and 2004) run the check continuously every 8 ms with the engine running: a fault is recorded once measured pressure stays more than 3.0 MPa above the target for longer than 7 s, the reverse case being P2290.
s: Reduced power and rough idle
Engine runs on a substitute pressure value
MIL on
c: ICP sensor reading offset, including a shifted internal O-ring
Injection pressure regulator valve sticking or contaminated
Wrong, aerated or low engine oil disturbing pressure control
Oil wicking into the sensor connector

P2285.d: P2285 is set when the ICP sensor voltage falls almost to zero. Ford's 6.0L Power Stroke summaries for 2003 and 2004 define it precisely: below 0.03 V, checked every 8 ms without entry conditions, decided in under one second.
s: MIL on immediately
Hard starting and reduced power
c: Signal wire open or shorted to ground

P2286.d: P2286 means the ICP sensor voltage has risen to the top of the range. In Ford's 2004 summary for the 6.0L Power Stroke the limit is above 4.83 V, checked every 8 ms and confirmed in less than one second; the 2003 edition already names the code alongside P2285.
s: MIL on
Reduced power and possibly harsh running
c: Signal wire shorted to the 5-volt reference or another voltage
ICP sensor failed with output stuck high

P2287.d: P2287 covers an ICP sensor signal that drops out or jumps for brief moments, too short or too irregular to be judged as a steady low or high fault. No manufacturer documents P2287 publicly; Ford's 6.0L summaries and its 2014 PCM table contain the steady electrical codes P2285 and P2286 but not this one.
s: Occasional stumble, surge or hesitation
Code returns without a fault visible in the workshop
c: Engine oil creeping into the sensor connector
Fretting or loose terminals at sensor or PCM
Harness rubbing on engine parts and shorting briefly

P2288.d: P2288 reports that the injector control pressure itself, not just its reading, has climbed above the allowed maximum while the engine runs. Ford's 6.0L Power Stroke summaries put the limit at 27.5 MPa in the 2003 edition and 29.5 MPa in 2004, sustained for more than 3 s.
s: Reduced power with fuel limit active
Loud injection noise or knocking
MIL on
c: Injection pressure regulator valve stuck or contaminated
Fault in the regulator drive circuit holding it at high duty
ICP sensor reading higher than the actual pressure

P2289.d: P2289 is a plausibility test carried out with the engine stopped. On a HEUI diesel the high-pressure oil pump is driven by the engine, so once it stops, injector control pressure should drop to almost nothing.
s: MIL on, possibly after the engine was switched off
Hard starting if the PCM trusts the false pressure value
c: ICP sensor with a positive offset or oil contamination
Partial short between signal and reference voltage
Faulty input stage in the PCM

P228A.d: P228A is a protective shutdown code: the engine computer has stopped the engine because rail pressure could not be held even with fuel pressure regulator A at full authority. In GM's 2018 diesel tables regulator 1 (A) is the fuel metering unit on the high-pressure pump; the fault is logged when actual pressure lags the setpoint by more than 40 MPa while the commanded pump flow is already at its maximum, in 640 of 800
s: Engine stalls while driving or shuts off shortly after starting
Long cranking or no restart
Check engine light on, often with P0087
Whining in-tank fuel pump in cold weather
c: Fuel supply starved (gelled or waxed diesel, clogged filter, failing in-tank pump)
Fuel metering unit on the high-pressure pump sticking or worn
High-pressure pump no longer reaching the required delivery
Leak in the high-pressure circuit or injector return

P228B.d: P228B mirrors P228A but concerns fuel pressure regulator B, which in GM's 2018 diesel calibration is the rail pressure regulator valve that spills surplus fuel from the rail. The ECM shuts the engine down when rail pressure stays more than 40 MPa below target although it already commands that valve fully closed, judged over 640 of 800 samples at 12.5 ms and stored as Type A.
s: Engine stops on its own and may not restart
Check engine light with low rail pressure codes
Loss of power just before the shutdown
c: Rail pressure regulator valve not sealing when closed
Fuel starvation from gelled diesel or a blocked filter

P228C.d: P228C means rail pressure has stayed below target long enough that regulator A, the path that sets pump delivery, is judged to have used up its correction. GM uses it widely on gasoline direct injection: in table 25OBDG03A the pump fails to keep up for 10 s within a 12.5 s window, logged as Type A; on its 2018 diesels the margin is 13 MPa with the metering unit in closed loop (Type B), and table 24OBDG07 uses a 3 MPa
s: Reduced engine power message
Hesitation under load
Check engine light, sometimes clearing after a key cycle
