c: High-pressure pump or its control valve sticking or worn (e.g. after heavy E85 use)
Low-pressure supply too weak or contaminated fuel
Water or corrosion in the injector or pump wiring
Rail pressure sensor reading too low

P228D.d: P228D is the opposite of P228C: measured rail pressure stays above the setpoint for too long although regulator A should be cutting delivery. GM's gasoline table 25OBDG03A flags it when the high-pressure pump supplies more than requested for 10 of 12.5 s, as Type A; its 2018 diesel table uses minus 13 MPa with the metering unit in closed loop (Type B), and table 24OBDG07 minus 3 MPa for 7 s.
s: Check engine light
Louder injection noise or rough idle
Reduced power in some cases
c: Pump control or metering valve not reducing delivery
Engine control software needing an update
Rail pressure sensor reading too high
Defective unit or high-pressure pump (truck engines)

P228E.d: P228E reports that the self-learned correction of fuel pressure regulator A has reached its lower bound. Ford, which still calls the part regulator 1, explains the logic in its 2023 diesel summary for the 3.0 L and 6.7 L Power Stroke: whenever requested rail pressure is at least 600 bar, the PCM keeps adapting the pressure controller, and if the adaptation factor drifts beyond a limit equivalent to roughly a 20 % err
s: Check engine light without noticeable drivability change
Occasional rough running or slower pressure response
c: Pressure regulator or metering valve worn, characteristic changed
High-pressure pump delivery deviating from its model

P228F.d: P228F is the upper counterpart of P228E: the learned correction for fuel pressure regulator A has run into its maximum. Ford's 2023 diesel summary applies one test to both codes on the 3.0 L and 6.7 L engines, with a limit near a 20 % rail pressure sensor slope error and about 10 s of monitoring at 600 bar or more.
s: Check engine light
Noise from the high-pressure pump
Uneven running in some cases
c: Dirt in the high-pressure system, e.g. via a leaking fuel filter seal

P2290.d: P2290 belongs to the injector control pressure (ICP) family of hydraulically actuated unit injector (HEUI) diesels such as the Navistar-built Ford 6.0 L Power Stroke, where pressurised engine oil fires the injectors. Ford's 2003 and 2004 summaries run the check every 8 ms with the engine running and set it once actual ICP stays more than 3.0 MPa below the PCM's command for longer than 7 s; Ford's 2014 PCM code table
s: Hard starting, especially when hot
Lack of power and rough running
Check engine light
c: Injection pressure regulator (IPR) contaminated or not sealing
Leaking high-pressure oil rail fittings, stand pipes or O-rings
Low, wrong or aerated engine oil

P2291.d: P2291 judges pressure build-up while the starter is turning. On HEUI diesels the injectors only fire once injector control pressure has reached a minimum, so any leak in the pressurised oil circuit shows up as a long crank or a no-start; Wikipedia's Power Stroke article names a contaminated injection pressure regulator and failed high-pressure oil seals as typical no-start causes on the 6.0 L.
s: Engine cranks long or does not start
Starts only after repeated attempts
Check engine light after the start attempt
c: Leak in the high-pressure oil (HEUI) or fuel (common rail) circuit
Injection pressure regulator or rail pressure valve not sealing
High-pressure pump delivering too little at cranking speed
Low cranking speed from a weak battery or starter

P2292.d: P2292 describes an injector control pressure that jumps around instead of sitting steadily below or above target. No manufacturer documents its detection logic publicly: Ford's 2014 PCM code table lists the code without a MIL marking, and the 6.0 L Power Stroke summaries only describe the steady checks P2284, P2288 and P2290.
s: Surging or bucking under steady throttle
Intermittent power loss
Rough idle
c: Air in the engine oil (foaming, wrong oil, overfill)
ICP sensor or its connector making intermittent contact
High-pressure oil pump starting to fail

P2293.d: P2293 checks whether fuel pressure regulator B really controls rail pressure. In GM's 2018 diesel table regulator B is the rail pressure regulator valve; the code sets when, with that valve in charge, rail pressure rises above a calibrated ceiling of 67 to 217 MPa in 160 of 229 samples at 6.25 ms, Type A.
s: Check engine light
Reduced power or stalling in severe cases
Hard starting
c: Rail pressure regulator valve sticking or worn (often replaced with the rail)

P2294.d: P2294 is the open-circuit check of the drive line to fuel pressure regulator B. GM's 2018 diesel ECM tests the low-side driver of the rail pressure regulator valve while the output is switched off: a voltage indicating more than 200 kΩ between signal and ground counts as open, and 44 failures in 88 samples at 6.25 ms set the code as Type B.
s: Check engine light
Reduced power or emergency mode
Unstable idle or hard starting
c: Broken wire in the regulator harness
Loose, corroded or pushed-back connector pin
Open coil in the pressure regulator valve
Faulty output driver in the engine control module

P2295.d: P2295 stands for the control line of fuel pressure regulator B touching ground. GM's 2018 diesel ECM detects it with its low-side driver switched off: if the measured voltage corresponds to 0.5 Ω or less towards ground, the sample counts as failed, and 44 of 88 samples at 6.25 ms confirm the fault as Type B.
s: Check engine light
Rail pressure too high or unstable, reduced power
Rough running
c: Control wire chafed through to ground
Water or corrosion in the regulator connector
Shorted coil in the pressure regulator valve

P2296.d: P2296 is set when the control line of fuel pressure regulator B has contact with supply voltage. GM's 2018 diesel ECM checks this with its low-side driver switched on: if the line still shows a voltage equivalent to 0.5 Ω or less towards power, the sample fails, again with 44 of 88 samples and Type B.
s: Check engine light
Hard starting or stalling
Reduced power
c: Control wire shorted to a voltage supply
Faulty output driver in the engine control module

P2297.d: P2297 concerns the upstream oxygen sensor of bank 1 and the moment when fuel is cut on deceleration and the sensor should read almost pure air. Diesel calibrations compare the reading in overrun with a modelled value: GM's 6.6L LML faults a gap between measured and calculated value above 0.06 to 0.07, the 3.0L LZ0 a deviation beyond 5 percent (Type B).
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Usually no noticeable change in driving behaviour
Possibly stored with P0133 or fuel-quantity codes
c: Upstream wide-band sensor aged or drifted (wrong reading in air)
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor drawing in outside air
Air-mass or fuel model error (MAF, injector leakage, EGR) skewing the expected value
Engine software needing an update (GM 3.0L LZ0 2024, bulletin 24-NA-094)

P2298.d: P2298 is the bank 2 version of P2297 and exists only on engines with two cylinder banks, each with its own upstream oxygen sensor. Three GM tables show the two readings of the code.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Usually no noticeable change in driving behaviour
Bank 2 fuel trim values may look unusual
c: Bank 2 upstream wide-band sensor aged or contaminated
Exhaust leak on bank 2 ahead of the sensor
Damaged sensor lead or connector on bank 2

P2299.d: P2299 means the vehicle has seen the brake and the accelerator pressed together in a way it treats as implausible; engine torque is usually cut as a brake-override measure. GM documents the check in the brake control module of 2020 models with a pedal travel sensor: the code sets when the travel signal is not zero while the accelerator is applied above 4.47 mph (7.2 km/h) for 0.12 s, Type A.
s: Engine power drops while braking and accelerating together
Check engine light
Car does not respond to the accelerator for a moment
c: Driver resting a foot on the brake while accelerating
Control module software needing an update
Brake light switch or pedal travel sensor misadjusted or sticking
Floor mat or object keeping a pedal partly pressed

P229A.d: P229A is the low-pressure control-limit check for fuel pressure regulator B. In GM's 2018 diesel table regulator B is the rail pressure regulator valve; while it governs the rail in closed loop, the ECM compares setpoint and measured pressure and flags a deficit beyond about 13 MPa, using the same 640-of-800-sample window and Type B rating as the metering unit check P228C.
s: Check engine light
Lack of power under load
Longer cranking times
c: Rail pressure regulator valve leaking internally
Restricted low-pressure supply or clogged filter

P229B.d: P229B flags rail pressure that stays above target while fuel pressure regulator B should be holding it. GM's 2018 diesel table, where regulator B is the rail pressure regulator valve, runs this check with the valve in closed-loop control and under the same enable conditions as P229A (fuel level, ambient pressure and temperature), mirroring the overpressure test P228D of the metering unit, and rates it Type B.
s: Check engine light
Harder combustion noise
Reduced power in some cases
c: Rail pressure regulator valve sticking closed
Rail pressure sensor reading too high
Valve drive signal stuck on (wiring or module)

P229C.d: P229C means the learned correction for fuel pressure regulator B has reached its lower bound. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Check engine light
Usually no noticeable change in driving
c: Rail pressure regulator valve characteristic drifted
Adaptation values not reset after a component replacement

P229D.d: P229D reports that the learned correction for fuel pressure regulator B has climbed to its upper bound, the opposite of P229C. No manufacturer documents the code publicly, so its logic can only be inferred from the regulator A equivalent P228F: Ford's 2023 diesel summary sets that code after about 10 s when the controller adaptation passes a limit near a 20 % sensor-slope error, and Volvo and Mack link P228F on their
s: Check engine light
Occasional unstable rail pressure or rough idle
c: Rail pressure regulator valve worn or contaminated
Contaminated fuel reaching the high-pressure side

P229E.d: P229E is the basic electrical fault of the second NOx sensor on bank 1, the one behind the SCR catalyst that shows how much NOx survives conversion. Its attached control unit checks the probe lines and passes the result to the engine computer over CAN.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
No valid downstream NOx value in live data
SCR warning; catalyst efficiency check cannot complete
c: Internal failure of the outlet NOx probe or its control unit
Damaged lead between probe and sensor control unit (heat, chafing)
Water or corrosion in the sensor connector
Engine control software needing an update (Nissan Titan XD 2016, NTB16-048)

P229F.d: P229F says the rear NOx sensor on bank 1 is electrically sound but its reading fails a plausibility test. Methods vary.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Often stored together with SCR efficiency code P20EE
Downstream NOx value implausible compared with the upstream sensor
c: Outlet NOx element drifted, slow or poisoned (e.g. sodium from cleaning fluids)
Poor DEF quality or faulty dosing that distorts downstream NOx
Harness or connector fault at the outlet sensor (Volvo/Mack P229F-64)
Engine or dosing software needing an update (several FCA, Hino, Mazda notices)

P22A0.d: P22A0 reports that the rear NOx sensor on bank 1 sends a raw value below the smallest figure a healthy sensor can produce. Because the sensor talks over CAN, the test looks at the transmitted number rather than a wire voltage.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Live data shows a negative downstream NOx value
SCR efficiency monitor does not complete
c: Outlet NOx element drifted low or internally faulty
Damaged lead between probe and sensor module

P22A1.d: P22A1 flags a raw value from the rear NOx sensor on bank 1 that is higher than anything plausibly left behind the SCR catalyst. GM's 6.6L LML uses 1,500 ppm, or 2,500 ppm in table 14OBDG10; the 3.0L LZ0 and the 2017 small diesels also use 2,500 ppm, Type B after two trips.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Implausibly high downstream NOx value in live data
SCR efficiency code P20EE stored alongside
c: Outlet NOx sensor reading high due to internal damage
DEF quality or dosing problem raising real tailpipe NOx

P22A2.d: P22A2 describes a rear NOx sensor on bank 1 whose measuring circuit reports faults that come and go rather than staying present. Smart NOx sensors pass the state of that circuit (open wire, short or no error) to the engine computer over CAN, so brief, repeated fault reports fit this code.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp that may go out and return
Downstream NOx value dropping out briefly
Code remains stored after the root fault is fixed
c: Loose or corroded terminals at the outlet NOx sensor connector
Harness along the exhaust damaged by heat or vibration
Sporadic internal fault in the sensor module

P22A3.d: The ceramic element of a NOx sensor measures only after its built-in heater has brought it to several hundred degrees. P22A3 reports a break on the heater control side of the rear sensor on bank 1, behind the SCR catalyst.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after one trip
Outlet NOx sensor never reports ready
SCR warning on the display
c: Heater element in the outlet NOx probe burnt through
Broken conductor between probe and sensor module

P22A4.d: P22A4 means the heater control line of the rear NOx sensor on bank 1 has a short to ground, so the sensor module can no longer drive the heater as commanded. GM documents it on the 3.0L LZ0 as a ground short on the heater control pin, judged once dew point is reached and sensor supply exceeds 9.9 V, 80 failures in 160 samples, Type B after two trips.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Outlet NOx sensor stays not ready
SCR warning on the display
c: Heater element or probe lead shorted to ground inside the sensor
Probe lead insulation chafed against the exhaust or body

P22A5.d: P22A5 is the opposite of P22A4: the heater control line of the rear NOx sensor on bank 1 has a short to supply voltage. The sensor module then cannot switch or regulate the heater, and the element risks running too hot or the module shuts the heater off to protect it.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Heater switched off, outlet NOx sensor not ready
SCR warning on the display
c: Heater circuit inside the sensor shorted to supply voltage
Probe lead or connector touching a powered conductor

P22A6.d: Besides the heater supply, a NOx sensor has a sense line through which its module measures the resistance of the heated element and so infers its temperature. P22A6 reports an electrical fault on that feedback line of the rear sensor on bank 1.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after one trip
Outlet NOx sensor not ready, no downstream value
SCR warning on the display
c: Open heater sense conductor inside the outlet NOx probe or its lead
Water or corrosion in the probe connector

P22A7.d: P22A7 means the heater feedback of the rear NOx sensor on bank 1 shows a heater that does not reach or hold its target, although no open or short is found. GM's 3.0L LZ0 and 2017 small diesels compare the measured heater resistance with its target once supply has been in range for 45 s and dew point passed 180 s ago (Type B); the 6.6L LML fails the sensor if its heater never reports set-point temperature.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Outlet NOx sensor becomes ready late or not at all
Often stored with U029E or other NOx sensor codes
c: Aged heater or element in the outlet NOx probe
Water in the NOx sensor connectors (Ford 6.7L 2017-2020, TSB 20-2067)
Harness chafed on the EGR cooler with blown supply fuse (Ford 6.7L 2023)
Weak supply to the sensor module limiting heater power

P22A8.d: P22A8 means the heater sense line of the rear NOx sensor on bank 1 is shorted to ground; the sensor module uses that line to read the element temperature via its resistance. With that line pulled to ground, the module sees a temperature value it cannot trust and cannot regulate the heater properly.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Outlet NOx sensor not ready
SCR efficiency check does not run
c: Heater sense conductor shorted to ground inside the probe
Probe lead insulation damaged against exhaust or body
Water bridging pins in the probe connector

P22A9.d: P22A9 is the high-side twin of P22A8: the heater sense line of the rear NOx sensor on bank 1 has a short to supply voltage. The module then reads an element resistance that is far off and loses its temperature feedback, so it cannot hold the probe at working temperature.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Outlet NOx sensor not ready
SCR warning on the display
c: Heater sense conductor shorted to supply inside the probe
Probe lead touching another powered conductor
Water bridging pins in the probe connector

P22AA.d: P22AA covers a heater sense line on the rear NOx sensor of bank 1 that fails only now and then. The module uses this line to read the element temperature and keep the heater on target; if the reading drops out or jumps for short moments, the temperature control briefly loses its reference and the sensor may fall out of its ready state.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp that may come and go
Outlet NOx sensor intermittently not ready
c: Loose or corroded terminal in the probe connector
Lead near the exhaust cracked by heat or vibration
Intermittent internal contact fault in the probe

P22AB.d: P22AB reports a break in the positive current control line of a wide-band probe mounted behind the catalyst or, on diesels, further down the aftertreatment on bank 1. On a Bosch-style five-wire probe this is the pump-current lead (IP/APE) through which the controller moves oxygen into or out of the pump cell.
s: Check engine light
Downstream oxygen reading frozen or missing in live data
Related catalyst or aftertreatment monitors stay incomplete
c: Corroded, loose or poorly crimped terminal in the sensor or sensor-module connector
Pump-current wire broken or chafed through along the exhaust
Internal open circuit in the downstream wide-band sensor

P22AC.d: P22AC means the pump-current (positive current) line of the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe reads below its allowed window, usually because the wire touches ground or its insulation has worn through. GM includes the code in bulletin 21-NA-149 for 2019-2022 light-duty trucks and SUVs with the 3.0 Duramax LM2, where chafed engine wiring triggers a long list of faults; no public GM table gives a threshold.
s: Check engine light
Downstream oxygen value pinned at an extreme in live data
Possible failed emissions inspection because monitors are not ready
c: Pump-current wire chafed against the body or exhaust and shorted to ground
Internal short in the downstream wide-band sensor
Water or contamination bridging the connector pins

P22AD.d: P22AD is the high-side fault on the positive current control line of the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe: the pump-current wire is pulled above its expected level, for example by contact with the heater feed or another supply wire. On Saab's 2010 9-5 the pump-current pins measure roughly 2.8 V at the plug, which gives a feel for the normal bias.
s: Check engine light
Downstream oxygen reading implausibly high or fixed
Readiness monitors for catalyst or aftertreatment not completed
c: Pump-current wire shorted to the heater supply or another positive feed
Internal short between heater and pump cell in the sensor
Faulty sensor interface in the ECM or sensor module

P22AE.d: P22AE points to an open reference voltage line of the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe, i.e. the lead of the Nernst (sensing) cell, called RE/UN by Bosch and VS by NTK.
s: Check engine light
Downstream oxygen or lambda value invalid in live data
Other downstream sensor codes may be stored at the same time
c: Corroded or wrongly plated terminals in the sensor or sensor-module connector
Broken Nernst-cell wire in the harness
Cracked or aged sensing cell with very high internal resistance

P22AF.d: P22AF is a plausibility fault on the Nernst-cell (reference voltage) side of the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe: the wiring is intact, but the cell signal does not behave as the controller expects, for instance it cannot be held at its set point or drifts. Typical reasons are an aged cell whose resistance has risen above the roughly 300 ohms Bosch quotes for the LSU 4.9, soot or oil deposits, or a heater that keep
s: Check engine light
Downstream oxygen reading sluggish or offset compared with the upstream sensor
Catalyst or aftertreatment monitor may report errors as a follow-up
c: Aged downstream wide-band sensor with raised cell resistance
Soot, oil or coolant deposits on the sensing element
Weak heater or heater control that leaves the element too cold
High-resistance contact in the Nernst-cell circuit

P22B0.d: P22B0 says the reference voltage (Nernst-cell) line of the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe sits below its permitted range. On a Bosch LSU the Nernst cell is a high-impedance source that tolerates at most about 250 microamps, so a chafed wire touching ground drags it down at once.
s: Check engine light
Downstream oxygen value implausible or unavailable
c: Nernst-cell wire shorted to ground through damaged insulation
Internal short in the downstream wide-band sensor
Moisture in the connector creating a leakage path

P22B1.d: P22B1 is set when the reference voltage (Nernst-cell) line of the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe reads above its valid range. Because the cell delivers only a few hundred millivolts across about 300 ohms, any contact with the heater feed or another live wire overrides it.
s: Check engine light
Downstream oxygen reading stuck at a limit
c: Nernst-cell wire shorted to the heater supply or another live wire
Cracked sensor ceramic leaking heater voltage into the cell
Faulty sensor interface in the ECM or sensor module

P22B2.d: P22B2 indicates an open negative current control line on the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe. This is the shared return of pump and sensing cell, the virtual ground (VM/IPN on Bosch, COM on NTK), which the controller holds at a mid-level bias of around 2.5 V.
s: Check engine light
Downstream oxygen reading frozen near a fixed value
Aftertreatment readiness not set
c: Loose, corroded or pushed-back terminal on the return wire
Return (virtual ground) wire broken in the harness
Internal open circuit in the downstream wide-band sensor

P22B3.d: P22B3 reports the negative current control line, i.e. the virtual ground of the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe, as too low.
s: Check engine light
Downstream oxygen value implausible or pinned
c: Return wire shorted to chassis ground through chafed insulation
Internal short inside the wide-band sensor
Faulty bias supply in the ECM or sensor module

P22B4.d: P22B4 is stored when the negative current control line (virtual ground) of the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe climbs above its intended bias. Because this return sits at a mid-level voltage rather than at chassis ground, a short to the heater feed or battery voltage is the classic trigger, sometimes via moisture or a heat-damaged connector.
s: Check engine light
Downstream oxygen reading erratic or at a limit
c: Return wire shorted to heater supply or battery voltage
Heat-damaged or wet connector bridging pins
Internal heater-to-cell leakage in the sensor

P22B5.d: P22B5 flags an open trim line on the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe. Bosch LSU probes carry a trimming resistor in the connector module, wired to pin 5 (RT/IA), that sets each sensor's individual characteristic; the controller reads it to scale the measured pump current.
s: Check engine light
Downstream oxygen reading disagrees with the upstream sensor during fuel cut-off
Follow-up aftertreatment or catalyst faults possible
c: Corroded or loose trim-line terminal in the sensor connector
Trim wire broken between sensor connector and ECM or sensor module
Open trimming resistor in the sensor's connector module

P22B6.d: By its name P22B6 is the low fault on the trim line of the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe, i.e. the lead to the calibration resistor in a Bosch-style sensor connector.
s: Check engine light
Negative oxygen percentage shown for the downstream sensor in live data
Possible additional boost or air-flow codes when charge air leaks
c: Faulty downstream NOx/oxygen sensor delivering an impossible oxygen value
Trim or signal wire shorted to ground in the harness

P22B7.d: P22B7 is, going by its title, the high fault on the trim circuit belonging to bank 1's downstream wide-band probe. In GM's diesel tables (2016, 2018 and 2025 group 04) the code is a ceiling test on the oxygen value of the second NOx sensor: the 2016 table flags readings above 24 %, which is more oxygen than fresh air holds, in 100 of 200 samples.
s: Check engine light
Downstream oxygen value above 21 % in live data
c: Faulty downstream NOx/oxygen sensor reporting excess oxygen
Chafed engine harness affecting the sensor lines (GM 3.0 LM2)
Trim or signal wire shorted to a voltage source

P22B8.d: P22B8 is the bank 2 version of an open positive current control line on a downstream wide-band probe: the pump-current wire (IP/APE on Bosch) of the sensor behind the catalyst or aftertreatment on the second cylinder bank has lost continuity. It only exists on engines with two exhaust banks and a wide-band probe after each catalyst, which is rare.
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 downstream oxygen value missing or frozen
c: Loose or corroded pump-current terminal in the sensor connector
Pump-current wire broken near the hot exhaust
Internal open circuit in the bank 2 downstream sensor

P22B9.d: P22B9 means the positive current control (pump-current) line of the bank 2 downstream wide-band probe reads below its allowed band, most often because the lead has worn through and touches ground. No maker documents this code publicly, so the logic can only be inferred from the bank 1 and upstream relatives: GM lists P22AC for the 3.0 Duramax LM2 without a threshold, Saab treats the upstream P2238 as a Type B fault,
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 downstream oxygen value at an extreme
c: Pump-current wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Internal short in the bank 2 downstream sensor

P22BA.d: P22BA is set when the pump-current (positive current control) wire of the bank 2 downstream wide-band probe is held above its normal bias, typically through contact with the heater supply or a damaged connector letting battery voltage in. No maker documents this code publicly.
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 downstream oxygen value implausibly high
c: Pump-current wire shorted to the heater feed or battery voltage
Faulty sensor interface in the ECM

P22BB.d: P22BB reports an open reference voltage line on the bank 2 downstream wide-band probe, meaning the controller has lost the Nernst-cell signal (RE/UN on Bosch, VS on NTK) it needs to regulate pump current and compute oxygen content. No maker documents this code publicly.
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 downstream oxygen value invalid
c: Corroded or loose Nernst-cell terminal in the connector
Reference wire broken in the harness
Cracked sensing cell or internal open in the sensor

P22BC.d: P22BC concerns the plausibility of the Nernst-cell signal of the wide-band probe fitted after the bank 2 catalyst. The leads test fine, yet the cell voltage that the controller uses as its set point drifts, reacts slowly or cannot be held, so the computed oxygen value loses credibility.
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 downstream oxygen reading lags behind or is offset from the other sensors
Catalyst monitor for bank 2 does not complete
c: Aged downstream wide-band sensor on bank 2 with raised Nernst-cell resistance
Oil, coolant or additive deposits on the sensing element
Heater output too low to keep the cell at working temperature
Contact resistance in the Nernst-cell terminal

P22BD.d: P22BD reports that the Nernst-cell (reference voltage) lead of the bank 2 post-catalyst wide-band probe sits below its valid window. Bosch allows the cell a load of only about 250 microamps, so a lead whose insulation touches ground, or moisture bridging the plug, pulls the signal down quickly.
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 downstream oxygen value missing or at the lower end in live data
c: Nernst-cell lead chafed through and touching ground
Water or corrosion creating a leakage path in the connector
Sensing element cracked by water contact on the hot probe

P22BE.d: P22BE is stored when the reference voltage lead of the bank 2 downstream wide-band probe carries more voltage than a working Nernst cell can produce. A healthy cell produces well under one volt from a source of roughly 300 ohms, so contact with the heater feed, a 5 V line or battery voltage swamps it, and a cracked ceramic can let heater potential leak into the cell.
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 downstream oxygen reading pinned at the upper limit
Heater codes for the same sensor may appear alongside
c: Nernst-cell lead shorted to the heater supply or another live wire
Cracked ceramic letting heater voltage into the sensing cell
Faulty sensor interface in the engine control module

P22BF.d: P22BF means the negative current control lead of the bank 2 post-catalyst wide-band probe has lost continuity. That lead is the common return of pump and Nernst cell (VM/IPN on Bosch, COM on NTK); without it neither cell has a reference and the signal freezes near its bias.
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 downstream oxygen value frozen at a constant reading
Further codes for the same sensor may be stored together
c: Loose, corroded or pushed-out terminal on the return wire
Return wire broken by heat or vibration near the exhaust
Internal break in the sensor lead or element

P22C0.d: P22C0 flags the negative current control line (virtual ground) of the bank 2 downstream wide-band probe as too low. The controller deliberately lifts this return above chassis ground, around 2.5 V on Saab's 2010 9-5, which lets the pump cell be driven both ways; once the wire touches ground, that bias and the lean side of the measuring range disappear.
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 downstream reading cannot show lean values
Readiness for catalyst and oxygen sensor monitors stays open
c: Return wire chafed against body or exhaust bracket, shorted to ground
Internal short from the sensor return to the housing
Faulty bias supply in the engine control module

P22C1.d: P22C1 covers a return line (virtual ground) reading too high on the bank 2 post-catalyst wide-band probe: the line is pushed above the mid-level bias the controller sets, which in practice means contact with the heater supply or battery voltage, often via a melted or wet connector. With the reference raised, the rich side of the scale is lost and the oxygen value becomes useless.
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 downstream reading stuck high or implausible
c: Return wire touching the heater feed or another positive supply
Heat-damaged or wet connector bridging the return to a live pin
Internal leakage from heater to sensing cells inside the probe

P22C2.d: P22C2 reports an open trim line on the bank 2 downstream wide-band probe. Every probe ships with a calibration resistor in its plug (pin 5, RT/IA on a Bosch LSU) that corrects for spread in its diffusion gap; on Bosch probes it sits in parallel with the controller's sense resistor.
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 downstream lambda reads slightly off, most visibly away from lambda 1
c: Corroded or loose trim-resistor terminal in the sensor plug
Trim resistor or its lead open inside the sensor connector
Trim wire broken between connector and control module

P22C3.d: P22C3 is the low fault on the trim (label resistor) circuit of the bank 2 post-catalyst wide-band probe. Ford's 2012 OBD summary shows how makers can read this for NTK probes: at each key-on the controller switches the heater off, samples a voltage divider and estimates the label resistor; a value too high is taken as a broken or grounded lead and sets the trim-low code (P2630 for the bank 2 front probe).
s: Check engine light
Code typically appears right after engine start
c: Trim wire chafed and shorted to ground
High-resistance or corroded trim terminal raising the measured resistance
Defective label resistor in the sensor connector

P22C4.d: P22C4 is the high fault on the trim circuit of the bank 2 downstream wide-band probe. In Ford's key-on check of NTK label resistors, an estimated resistance that is too low means the line is shorted to power, which sets the trim-high code (P2631 for the bank 2 front probe); the stored resistor rank then stays in use.
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 downstream lambda slightly off; heater codes may accompany it
c: Trim wire shorted to the heater supply or another positive feed
Heat- or water-damaged sensor plug bridging the trim pin
Internally shorted label resistor in the sensor connector

P22C5.d: P22C5 flags an open or broken drive circuit for the turbocharger compressor outlet valve. That valve sits in the charge-air path downstream of a compressor and decides whether this compressor feeds the engine, for example in register or two-stage charging or next to an electric auxiliary compressor.
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power because boost is limited
Weak or delayed pull at the speed where the second boost path should join
c: Valve connector loose, unplugged or corroded
Broken wire in the valve harness, often near hot turbo parts
Open actuator coil inside the compressor outlet valve
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P22C6.d: P22C6 is stored when the control line of the compressor outlet valve sits at a voltage that is too low for the current command, which normally points to a short to ground somewhere between the module and the valve. Whether the valve then stays permanently energized or never moves depends on whether the engine control module switches the ground side or the supply side of the coil.
s: Check engine light on soon after starting
Boost limited, engine feels flat under load
Possible blown fuse if the short pulls heavy current
c: Control wire chafed through and touching ground
Internal short in the valve actuator coil
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the connector
Damaged output stage in the engine control module

P22C7.d: P22C7 means the drive line of the compressor outlet valve reads higher than the module expects, typically because the wire has a short to battery voltage or the coil draws excessive current while the driver is on. Modern output stages notice the overcurrent and switch off to protect themselves, so the valve then stops responding even though nothing is open.
s: Check engine light on
Valve no longer switches, boost reduced
Code returns immediately after clearing
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage feed
Shorted turns in the valve coil causing overcurrent
Replacement valve with unsuitable coil resistance
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P22C8.d: P22C8 is a functional fault: the compressor outlet valve stays open at a moment when the control strategy expects it shut, so pressure or airflow in the boost path does not follow the command. Mercedes-Benz uses it on the M256.8 inline six with its 48-volt electric auxiliary compressor.
s: Check engine light on
Little or poor power output
Boost builds poorly or unevenly
c: Check valve in the charge-air pipe jammed (Mercedes M256)
Oil film or deposits holding the valve flap open
Actuator or linkage no longer able to close the valve

P22C9.d: P22C9 says the compressor outlet valve did not open when commanded, so air from the compressor it controls cannot reach the engine and the expected boost is missing. Mercedes-Benz documents the code for the M256.8 six-cylinder: the first version of bulletin LI09.41-P-078735 (December 2024) covers P22C900 in the MRG3 engine control unit on models from 2019 to 2025 and traces it to a check valve in the charge-air pipe
s: Check engine light on
Noticeable loss of power under load
Boost malfunction, possibly with underboost code
c: Check valve in the charge-air pipe jammed shut (Mercedes M256)
Valve actuator, vacuum or pressure supply unable to open the valve
Valve seized by deposits or corrosion

P22CA.d: P22CA reports an open drive circuit for the compressor outlet switching valve. In two-stage or register boost systems the outlet flap is often moved by vacuum or pressure, and this electrically driven switching valve decides when that actuating medium reaches it; Ford's two-stage patent notes such valves may be worked electrically or by vacuum.
s: Check engine light on
Boost changeover no longer happens, power limited
Hesitation when accelerating through the switching speed
c: Switching valve connector loose or corroded
Broken wire between module and switching valve
Open coil in the switching solenoid
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P22CB.d: P22CB is set when the control line of the compressor outlet switching valve shows too little voltage for the present command, most often because the wire or the solenoid has a short to ground. On a low-side driven solenoid such a short can hold the valve energized all the time, so the outlet flap it supplies with vacuum or pressure stays in its switched position whatever the rpm and load.
s: Check engine light on
Boost path stuck in one mode, uneven power across the rev range
Reduced power at low or high engine speed
c: Control wire chafed and shorted to ground
Internal short in the switching solenoid
Water or corrosion in the solenoid connector

P22CC.d: P22CC indicates that the drive line of the compressor outlet switching valve carries more voltage or current than allowed, usually a short to a battery feed or a solenoid with shorted windings. The output stage of the engine control module then tends to shut down for self-protection, which leaves the switching valve unpowered and the outlet flap in its rest position.
s: Check engine light on
Outlet flap no longer switches, power reduced
Fault returns as soon as the valve is commanded
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage feed
Shorted windings in the switching solenoid
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P22CD.d: P22CD is a plausibility fault: the engine control module commanded the compressor outlet switching valve shut, yet boost pressure, airflow or a position signal behave as if the switched path were still open. Because the switching valve feeds the actuator of the outlet flap, a mechanically stuck solenoid, a leaking control hose or a flap held open by the actuator all lead to the same result.
s: Check engine light on
Sluggish boost build-up at low engine speed
Hissing or whistling noise from the intake side
c: Switching solenoid mechanically stuck in the open position
Leaking, cracked or swapped control hose to the flap actuator
Outlet flap or its actuator unable to close

P22CE.d: P22CE is set when the compressor outlet switching valve was told to open but the boost system shows no sign that the switched path changed over. Nissan documents the code as TC Outlet Switching Valve Stuck Closed for the 2016 Titan XD with the Cummins 5.0 litre V8 diesel and its two-stage turbocharger.
s: Check engine light on, mostly in cold weather
Hesitation when accelerating until the engine is warm
Weak pull in the speed range where the second stage should help
c: Engine control software reacting wrongly in cold weather (Nissan Titan XD bulletin)
Collapsed, kinked or frozen control hose to the outlet flap actuator
Switching solenoid stuck in the closed position
Insufficient vacuum or pressure supply for the actuator

P22CF.d: P22CF points to an open drive circuit of the turbocharger turbine inlet valve, the exhaust-side valve that either lets gas skip the small first-stage turbine of a series two-stage system or isolates a second turbine in a parallel-sequential layout. GM's diesel OBD tables (17OBDG04 and 18OBDG04) group P22CF, P22D0 and P22D1 as the faults of the high-pressure turbine bypass actuator (HTB); while one is active, boost co
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power, boost control in fallback mode
Turbo lag or a missing second-stage push
c: Actuator connector loose, heat-damaged or corroded
Broken wire near the exhaust manifold or turbo
Open winding in the turbine valve actuator or its control solenoid
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P22D0.d: P22D0 is logged when the drive circuit of the turbine inlet valve shows a voltage below the expected range, the classic sign of a short to ground in the wire or inside the actuator. GM lists P22D0 together with P22CF and P22D1 in the fault bundle of its high-pressure turbine bypass actuator in the 2017 and 2018 diesel OBD documents; any of them takes boost control out of closed loop.
s: Check engine light on
Power limited, boost too low or uneven
Code sets right after start without a test drive
c: Heat-damaged wire rubbing through to ground
Internal short in the valve actuator or control solenoid
Damaged output stage in the engine control module

P22D1.d: P22D1 tells you the drive circuit of the turbine inlet valve reads too high, which usually means a short to battery voltage or an actuator that draws overcurrent. GM assigns P22D1, along with P22CF and P22D0, to its high-pressure turbine bypass actuator in the 2017 and 2018 diesel OBD tables, and boost control drops out of closed loop when the fault is active.
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power, boost control in fallback mode
Fault comes back as soon as the valve is driven
c: Actuator wire shorted to a battery-voltage feed
Actuator winding shorted or mechanically jammed, drawing overcurrent
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P22D2.d: P22D2 means the turbine inlet valve stays open after the module asked it to close. In a series two-stage system, an open valve lets exhaust skip the small high-pressure turbine, so low-speed boost and response suffer.
s: Check engine light on
Noticeable turbo lag at low engine speed
Higher fuel consumption
Reduced power mode
c: Soot or corrosion seizing the valve shaft in the open position
Leaking or detached control line on a vacuum-operated actuator
Actuator or linkage unable to close the valve
Position sensor reporting open although the valve moved

P22D3.d: P22D3 is stored when the turbine inlet valve does not open on command. In a series two-stage layout all exhaust must then pass the small high-pressure stage even at high load, raising back-pressure and risking overboost or turbo overspeed, so the module caps power.
s: Check engine light on
Power capped at higher engine speed and load
Possible overboost code alongside
c: Engine software setting the code falsely (Jeep Cherokee 2026 bulletin)
Valve seized closed by soot or corrosion
Actuator, linkage or vacuum supply unable to open the valve

P22D4.d: P22D4 is the general circuit fault of the sensor that reports how far the turbine inlet valve is open. Engineering literature explains why this valve, unlike most compressor bypass valves, has feedback: a Ford two-stage patent calls the high-pressure turbine bypass valve emissions-critical and therefore actively controlled with a position sensor, and a GM patent uses the measured opening to run the valve in position
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power, turbo valve held in a fallback position
c: Loose, heat-damaged or corroded sensor connector
Damaged sensor wiring near the turbo
Failed position sensor, often integrated in the actuator

P22D5.d: P22D5 is a plausibility fault of the turbine inlet valve position signal. The voltage stays inside its electrical limits, yet it does not match what the module expects, for instance the reading lags the commanded position, fails to reach the learned end stops or does not change when the valve is moved.
s: Check engine light on
Jerky or delayed changeover between turbo stages
Boost fluctuates under steady throttle
c: Valve or linkage sluggish from soot, so position lags the command
Position sensor drifting or misaligned on the actuator
End positions not relearned after actuator replacement

P22D6.d: P22D6 is set when the position sensor signal of the turbine inlet valve falls below its lowest valid voltage. Position sensors on such actuators normally work on a 5-volt reference with a signal that never reaches the rails in normal use, so a reading near zero means a lost reference, a signal wire shorted to ground or an internal sensor fault rather than a real valve position.
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power, valve in fallback position
Other sensor codes on the same reference circuit possible
c: 5-volt reference open or pulled down by another shorted sensor
Internal failure of the position sensor

P22D7.d: P22D7 is logged when the position signal of the turbine inlet valve rises above its highest valid voltage. A reading pinned near the reference level usually comes from an open sensor ground, a signal wire touching the 5-volt reference or battery voltage, or a failed sensor element, not from the valve itself.
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power, valve held in fallback position
c: Signal wire shorted to the 5-volt reference or battery voltage
Internal failure of the position sensor

P22D8.d: P22D8 covers short dropouts or jumps in the position signal of the turbine inlet valve: the value leaps faster than the valve could physically move, or briefly disappears and returns. Such patterns typically come from a connector with fretting contacts, a wire breaking inside its insulation near the vibrating, hot turbo, or a sensor that fails under heat.
s: Check engine light on, sometimes only now and then
Boost surging or hunting
Brief loss of power on rough roads
c: Loose or fretting contacts in the sensor connector
Wire breaking intermittently from heat and vibration
Position sensor dropping out when hot

P22D9.d: P22D9 reports a broken control circuit at the gas injector of cylinder 1, the solenoid that meters CNG or LPG into the intake port whenever a bi-fuel or dedicated gas engine runs on the alternative fuel. The driver stage notices the break because no current flows when it switches on, or because the expected off-state voltage on its pin is missing.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Engine changes back to gasoline or refuses to switch to gas
Misfire on cylinder 1 in gas mode (dedicated engines)
c: Open solenoid winding in the cylinder 1 gas injector
Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at the gas injector
Broken wire or failed splice in the gas system harness
Defective driver stage in the gas or engine control module

P22DA.d: P22DA means the cylinder 1 gas injector control wire reads too low. TransEco Energy's DTC list for its CNG control module (AFCM v1.4) blames either a grounded wire or an open line, turns on the MIL in bi-fuel installations and reacts the same way it would to the matching gasoline injector fault.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Very rough running on cylinder 1 in gas mode, possibly rich misfire
Gas system switches back to gasoline
c: Control wire of the cylinder 1 gas injector chafed through to ground
Interrupted control wire or connector (logged as Low by some modules)
Water or corrosion in the injector connector
Faulty output stage in the gas control module

P22DB.d: P22DB flags a control circuit of the cylinder 1 gas injector that stays too high. TransEco Energy's AFCM fault list traces it to a short to battery voltage, lights the MIL for bi-fuel use and applies the same fallback as for the gasoline injector fault; Ford's 2014 code list also marks P22DB for the MIL.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Lean misfire on cylinder 1 in gas mode, often with P0301
Engine runs normally on gasoline
c: Control wire shorted to battery or injector supply voltage
Shorted turns in the cylinder 1 gas injector coil
Output stage of the gas control module damaged

P22DC.d: P22DC is meant for a cylinder 1 gas injector whose circuit is electrically intact but whose response looks wrong, such as a current trace that never reaches its peak or does not fall back to the hold level, or a coil whose resistance has drifted. A Ford patent on driving a second type of injector through an interface (US 8,161,946) describes this logic: the injector counts as degraded if it ignores on and off command
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Uneven running in gas mode, misfire counts on cylinder 1
Higher gas consumption or switch back to gasoline
c: Cylinder 1 gas injector sticking from oil residue or debris in the gas
Injector coil resistance outside its specification
Weak supply voltage to the injector bank
Injector of the wrong type or impedance installed

P22DD.d: P22DD signals an interruption in the circuit of the cylinder 2 gas injector. On many systems that circuit is not driven by the engine computer: Ford's 2003 bi-fuel CNG trucks used a separate alternative fuel control module holding drivers for both injector sets, with heavier stages for the gas injectors because they draw more current.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Gas mode not available or ends shortly after switching
Misfire on cylinder 2 when running on gas
c: Burnt-out or open coil in the cylinder 2 gas injector
Connector at the cylinder 2 injector loose or pulled off
Wire break between gas control module and injector
Failed injector driver in the separate gas control module

P22DE.d: P22DE stands for a control line of the cylinder 2 gas injector whose voltage is too low. TransEco Energy's AFCM fault table blames a grounded or interrupted wire and turns on the MIL for bi-fuel vehicles; Ford's 2014 OBD code list includes P22DE as a MIL code too.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Rich misfire or fouled spark plug on cylinder 2 in gas mode
Gas operation interrupted, engine runs on gasoline
c: Cylinder 2 injector control wire grounded on engine or body
Open wire or pin, reported as Low by modules like the TransEco AFCM
Shorted output transistor in the gas control module

P22DF.d: P22DF indicates that the control circuit of the cylinder 2 gas injector reads high, which TransEco Energy's AFCM table attributes to a short to power; MIL on for bi-fuel use. Ford's 2014 code list likewise flags P22DF for the MIL.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Cylinder 2 misfires only on gas
Unexpected return to gasoline
c: Cylinder 2 control wire touching a live supply wire
Internal short in the cylinder 2 gas injector coil
Driver protection in the control module tripping due to a fault

P22E0.d: P22E0 covers a cylinder 2 gas injector circuit that passes the plain open and short checks yet responds outside its expected window. California's OBD regulation asks for output components to be checked not only for circuit faults but also for a proper functional response; for alternate-fueled vehicles from 2004 to 2018 the gasoline rules applied unchanged, and from 2019 the maker submits its own monitoring plan.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Uneven idle on gas, cylinder 2 misfire counts
Fuel trim drifts in gas mode
c: Cylinder 2 gas injector opening or closing too slowly
Coil resistance of the injector out of tolerance
Driver stage or supply unable to provide the required current

P22E1.d: P22E1 marks an open control circuit at the cylinder 3 gas injector. Circuit continuity checks of this kind run all the time: California's OBD rule defines continuous monitoring as always enabled with at least two samples per second, so a break is caught within moments once the gas system is in use.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Gas mode switches off soon after changeover
Cylinder 3 misfire on dedicated gas engines
c: Cylinder 3 injector connector left off or not latched after service
Open coil in the cylinder 3 gas injector
Wire broken where the harness runs along the gas rail

P22E2.d: P22E2 is logged when the control circuit of the cylinder 3 gas injector reads low. In TransEco Energy's AFCM table the cause column says shorted to ground or open, the MIL comes on in bi-fuel systems and the reaction copies that for a gasoline injector fault.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Cylinder 3 runs rich or misfires in gas mode
Smell of unburnt gas at the exhaust
c: Cylinder 3 control wire rubbed through against a bracket or the manifold
Broken wire or terminal in the cylinder 3 injector circuit
Shorted driver output in the gas control module

P22E3.d: P22E3 tells that the cylinder 3 gas injector circuit is held high. TransEco Energy's AFCM list names a short to power, MIL on for bi-fuel use, and Ford's 2014 code list also ties P22E3 to the MIL.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Lean misfire on cylinder 3 in gas mode, often with P0303
Noticeable loss of power on gas
c: Cylinder 3 control wire shorted to a 12 V feed
Shorted turns in the cylinder 3 gas injector
Faulty output of the injector control module

P22E4.d: P22E4 points to a cylinder 3 gas injector whose circuit works but whose electrical behaviour does not match the command. Peak-and-hold gas injectors first draw a high opening current and then a lower holding current; Ford's patent US 8,161,946 treats an injector that stays at peak or ignores commands as degraded and reports this back to the engine computer.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Intermittent cylinder 3 misfire on gas
Rising gas consumption
c: Armature of the cylinder 3 gas injector gummed up by oil or debris
Injector coil aged or overheated, resistance out of range
Weak driver output or poor supply ground

P22E5.d: P22E5 is the open-circuit code for the cylinder 4 gas injector; on four-cylinder gas engines it is the last injector of the set. The driver sees no current when it switches the injector on.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Gas mode unavailable, car runs on gasoline only
Cylinder 4 dead on a dedicated gas engine
c: Open coil in the cylinder 4 gas injector
Heat-damaged or brittle connector near the exhaust side
Broken wire in the cylinder 4 injector circuit

P22E6.d: P22E6 reports a low signal on the cylinder 4 gas injector control wire. TransEco Energy's AFCM table gives short to ground or open as the cause and turns the MIL on in bi-fuel installations, keeping the same failure response as for gasoline; Ford's 2014 code list carries P22E6 with the MIL as well.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Cylinder 4 runs rich or cuts out on gas
Engine stays on or returns to gasoline
c: Cylinder 4 control wire grounded through damaged insulation
Separated terminal or broken wire in the cylinder 4 circuit
Damaged driver output in the gas control module

P22E7.d: P22E7 says the control circuit of the cylinder 4 gas injector reads high. TransEco Energy's fault table blames a short to power and lights the MIL for bi-fuel use; Ford's 2014 code list also marks P22E7 as a MIL code.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Cylinder 4 misfire only after the switch to gas
Reduced power in gas mode
c: Cylinder 4 control wire in contact with a 12 V circuit
Cylinder 4 injector coil with internal short
Output stage of the controlling module defective

P22E8.d: P22E8 applies when the cylinder 4 gas injector circuit is complete but the measured response lies outside the plausible range, for instance an opening current that rises too slowly or a hold phase that never settles. No vehicle maker documents P22E8 openly; the published lists from TransEco and Ford end at Low/High.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Rough idle on gas, smooth on gasoline
Gas mode ends after a while
c: Cylinder 4 injector fouled by oil or liquids, often from a neglected gas filter
Aged injector coil with changed resistance
Low system voltage during cranking or at idle

P22E9.d: P22E9 is the open-circuit code for the cylinder 5 gas injector and can only appear on engines with five or more cylinders, such as the V6 of GM's bi-fuel Impala or the 6.0-litre V8 of its bi-fuel Silverado and Sierra. The driver detects the break because current is missing when the injector is commanded on.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Engine returns to gasoline after switching to gas
Cylinder 5 misfire if gas operation continues
c: Open coil in the cylinder 5 gas injector
Loose connector in the harness branch for this bank
Open driver output in the gas or injector control module

P22EA.d: P22EA stands for a low voltage on the cylinder 5 gas injector control wire, a code limited to engines with at least five cylinders. TransEco Energy's AFCM table points to a grounded wire or an open line, lights the MIL in bi-fuel use and applies the gasoline injector fault response; Ford's 2014 code list, written for V8 engines among others, keeps P22EA as a MIL code.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Cylinder 5 runs rich or misfires in gas mode
Fouled spark plug on cylinder 5
c: Cylinder 5 control wire shorted to ground along the gas rail
Interrupted wire or terminal, flagged as Low by some modules
Shorted output stage in the gas control module

P22EB.d: P22EB reports that the cylinder 5 gas injector control circuit is too high, which TransEco Energy's AFCM list attributes to a short to power with the MIL on for bi-fuel use; Ford's 2014 code list likewise carries P22EB for the MIL. The injector stays closed, so cylinder 5 burns no gas and misfires lean, usually logged together with P0305.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Lean misfire on cylinder 5 in gas mode, often with P0305
Normal running on gasoline
c: Cylinder 5 control wire chafed against a supply wire
Overheated cylinder 5 gas injector with shorted turns
Overloaded driver output in the gas control module

P22EC.d: P22EC is the plausibility code for the cylinder 5 gas injector circuit on engines with five or more cylinders: wiring and coil pass the basic checks, but the injector does not respond as commanded. California's OBD rule requires such output components to be checked for a proper functional response, and from model year 2019 the maker of an alternate-fueled vehicle submits its own plan for which monitors apply.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Rough cylinder 5 on gas or return to gasoline
Fuel trim on the affected bank drifts in gas mode
c: Sticking armature in the cylinder 5 gas injector
Driver or supply not delivering the full opening current

P22ED.d: P22ED marks an open control circuit at the cylinder 6 gas injector, the last injector on six-cylinder engines like the 3.6-litre V6 of GM's 2015 bi-fuel Impala, where the ECM drives the CNG injectors directly. Current is missing when the injector should open, so the module records the break.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Vehicle runs on gasoline although gas is selected
Cylinder 6 misfire on dedicated gas engines
c: Open coil in the cylinder 6 gas injector
Loose or corroded connector at cylinder 6
Broken wire between control module and cylinder 6 injector

P22EE.d: On engines that burn natural gas or propane through their own gas injectors, the control module watches the drive line of each gas valve. This code means the line to the cylinder 6 gas injector sits at a lower voltage than the switching state allows.
s: Check engine light on (bi-fuel versions)
Rough running or misfire on cylinder 6 in gas mode
System switches to gasoline or will not enter gas mode
c: Control wire of the cylinder 6 gas injector chafed through to ground
Broken wire or loose plug at the gas injector (counted as Low by this system)
Faulty output stage in the PCM or gas control module

P22EF.d: The counterpart to P22EE: the drive line of the cylinder 6 gas injector stays near battery voltage even when the output stage should pull it down. For Ford pickups and vans converted with the Altech-Eco/TransEco CNG kit, the installer sheet gives as cause is a short to power; the same MIL rule applies (on for bi-fuel, off for dedicated CNG), and the column for the gas module version 1.4 marks this fault as not detect
s: Check engine light on (bi-fuel versions)
Lean misfire on cylinder 6 in gas mode
Automatic change to gasoline operation
c: Control wire of the cylinder 6 gas injector touching a battery-voltage feed
Gas harness spliced or pinned incorrectly during the conversion
Moisture bridging supply and control pins in the injector plug
Output stage in the control module no longer switches

P22F0.d: Unlike the pure wiring faults P22EE/P22EF, this code is meant for a cylinder 6 gas injector circuit that is electrically intact but behaves implausibly, for example a current rise or switching response that does not fit the command. No manufacturer documents this code publicly: neither the Ford 2014 code list nor the Altech-Eco/TransEco CNG table contains it; both stop at Low and High for this cylinder.
s: Uneven idle or hesitation in gas mode
Cylinder 6 misfire count rising on gas only
Check engine light possible
c: Cylinder 6 gas valve sticking from oil or deposits carried in the gas
Coil resistance drifted out of the expected window
Corroded plug causing a slow current rise

P22F1.d: A general circuit or open-wire code for the gas injector of cylinder 7, which only exists on V8 and larger engines. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Misfire on cylinder 7 in gas mode
Fallback to gasoline on bi-fuel vehicles
Check engine light on
c: Plug of the cylinder 7 gas injector loose or left off after service
Broken control or supply wire in the gas harness

P22F2.d: Low voltage on the control line of the cylinder 7 gas injector. The code appears in Ford's 2014 code list with MIL and in the installer table of the Altech-Eco/TransEco CNG kits, which on Ford's V8 (F-150 5.0) and V10 (Super Duty 6.8) engines use the PCM to drive gas valves for all cylinders; cylinders 9 and 10 of the V10 get manufacturer codes there.
s: Check engine light on (bi-fuel versions)
Cylinder 7 misfire or rich running on gas
Gas mode blocked or ended
c: Cylinder 7 injector control wire grounded on the engine or bracket
Open wire or poor pin contact (reported as Low)

P22F3.d: Here the cylinder 7 gas valve drive line is held high, so the output stage cannot switch the valve on. Ford's 2014 list carries P22F3 with MIL; the Altech-Eco/TransEco table for its Ford V8 and V10 CNG systems names a short to power as cause, applies MIL only to bi-fuel trucks and notes that gas module version 1.4 cannot detect this fault itself.
s: Lean misfire on cylinder 7 in gas mode
Check engine light on (bi-fuel versions)
Gas operation dropped in favour of gasoline
c: Cylinder 7 control wire shorted to a switched or battery feed
Wiring error at the splice between factory and gas harness
Output stage in the control module open

P22F4.d: Plausibility code for the cylinder 7 gas injector circuit: wiring passes the open/short checks, yet the electrical response of the valve does not match what the driver expects. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Intermittent stumble in gas mode
Misfire code for cylinder 7 possible
Check engine light possible
c: Cylinder 7 gas valve slow or sticking from oil residue
Injector coil resistance shifted with heat or age
Weak supply voltage to the gas injector bank

P22F5.d: Open-circuit code for the gas injector of cylinder 8. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Cylinder 8 misfire whenever the engine runs on gas
Change to gasoline on bi-fuel vehicles
Check engine light on
c: Cylinder 8 injector plug corroded or disconnected
Wire fatigued at a flex point of the gas harness
Coil of the cylinder 8 gas valve open

P22F6.d: Cylinder 8 is the last cylinder with a generic gas injector code; beyond it the Altech-Eco/TransEco table for the Ford 6.8 V10 switches to manufacturer codes. P22F6 reports a control line for the cylinder 8 valve that is too low.
s: Check engine light on (bi-fuel versions)
Misfire on cylinder 8 only in gas mode
Gas mode not available
c: Cylinder 8 control wire grounded through damaged insulation
Open wire or unplugged injector (reported as Low)

P22F7.d: P22F7 means the drive line of the cylinder 8 gas injector cannot be pulled down and stays near supply voltage. Ford lists it with MIL in the 2014 code list; in the conversion data from Altech-Eco/TransEco the cause given is a short to power, keeps the MIL off on dedicated CNG engines and marks the fault as not detectable by gas module version 1.4.
s: Cylinder 8 lean misfire in gas mode
Check engine light on (bi-fuel versions)
Vehicle stays on gasoline
c: Cylinder 8 control wire pinched against a supply line
Supply and control pins swapped in the gas harness
Damaged output stage in the control module

P22F8.d: Functional code for the cylinder 8 gas injector circuit, meant for cases where wiring is intact but the valve reacts outside the expected window. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Hesitation under load in gas mode
Cylinder 8 misfire code possible
Check engine light possible
c: Cylinder 8 gas valve opening late or partly due to contamination
Coil degraded by heat at the rear of the engine
Contact resistance in the injector plug

P22F9.d: P22F9 concerns the NOx sensor ahead of the SCR catalyst on bank 1 and how fast it follows a rise in engine-out NOx. After a load step the control module times the sensor signal and compares it with the curve of its own NOx model.
s: Check engine light on after two drives
Usually no noticeable change in driving
SCR efficiency codes may follow
c: Front NOx sensor aged or contaminated (oil ash, silicone, cleaning agents), reacting slowly
ECM calibration error, fixed by reprogramming (GM 24-NA-058 for the 2024 L5P)
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor diluting the gas sample
Soot or deposits covering the protective cap of the sensor

P22FA.d: P22FA mirrors P22F9 for the falling edge: when engine-out NOx drops, mostly as the driver lifts off into overrun, the front NOx sensor on bank 1 takes too long to come down. GM's 2014 Cruze 2.0 diesel fails it when the signal needs more than 1.8 s between 30 and 60 % of its starting value at 1320 rpm or more; the 6.6L LML allows 2.3 s for a drop from 70 to 40 %.
s: Check engine light on
Warning about poor DEF quality on some GM diesels
Usually no change in engine behaviour
c: Engine software anomaly, cured by reprogramming (GM PI1485, FCA 18-018-15, 18-008-21)
Front NOx sensor aged or contaminated, signal decays slowly
Exhaust leak near the sensor disturbing the measurement

P22FB.d: P22FB questions whether the measuring element of the front NOx sensor on bank 1 still reads true. GM's 2025 diesel tables hold its filtered value against modelled engine-out NOx and fail it below minus 36 % or above plus 77 % (version A) or outside minus 51 to plus 100 % (version B), as a Type A fault with the MIL in one trip.
s: Check engine light on, on GM's 2025 diesels already after one drive
Rough idle or surging if an EGR fault is behind it
Often no other noticeable effect
c: Measuring cell of the front NOx sensor drifted or damaged (Volvo/Mack P22FB-92)
ECM or DEF control unit software, fixed by reprogramming (Isuzu SB22-L-001, GM 23-NA-159, Mazda 01-004-22)
Real engine-out NOx differs from the model, e.g. through an EGR fault (P0402)
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor

P22FC.d: P22FC is reserved for the rear NOx sensor on bank 1, behind the SCR catalyst, when its signal climbs too slowly after NOx at that point increases. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, and the NHTSA bulletin index has no entry for it.
s: Check engine light on
No change in driving behaviour
c: Rear NOx sensor aged or contaminated by urea deposits, oil ash or cleaning agents
Exhaust leak between SCR catalyst and sensor
Calibration of the test itself, check for software updates

P22FD.d: P22FD stands for the falling edge at the rear NOx sensor on bank 1: after a NOx peak downstream of the SCR catalyst, the signal decays more slowly than permitted. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, and no bulletin in the NHTSA index names it.
s: Check engine light on
SCR efficiency code may appear as well
c: Rear NOx sensor aged or coated, signal falls too slowly
Urea crystals around the sensor tip after dosing faults
Exhaust leak close to the outlet sensor

P22FE.d: P22FE tests the measuring cells of the rear NOx sensor on bank 1. On GM diesels the check runs after the engine is switched off: the sensor alters its internal pump currents so that about 1000 ppm of oxygen sits in the second cavity, and the result is compared with a reference written into its memory at the supplier.
s: Check engine light on
Code sets after shutdown, so it often appears at the next start
Driving behaviour unchanged
c: Measuring cavities of the rear NOx sensor clogged or cells drifted
ECM or DEF control unit software (GM PIP5615A, 23-NA-193, Isuzu SB22-L-001)
Contamination by urea residue, oil ash or additive cleaners

P22FF.d: Diesel engines raise exhaust temperature on purpose so the SCR catalyst can reduce NOx; this code reports that the gas entering the SCR stays too cold despite that. Ford describes it for the 6.7L and 3.2L diesels under its monitoring of the exhaust temperature controller: the measured SCR inlet value is compared with the setpoint, and the fault sets when it lags more than 80 °C behind for 300 s (2015 model year, roug
s: Check engine light on
Reduced NOx conversion, possible further SCR efficiency codes
Code returns after extended idling
c: Long idling or light-load operation keeps exhaust cold
Exhaust leak ahead of the SCR cools the gas or skews the reading
Exhaust temperature sensor reading too low while still in range
Engine software with overly strict monitor (update available on some makes)
